subjects.name: Physik
subjects.description: At Gymnasium Physik is a separate subject from Kl. 7 at the latest (NRW teaches it from Kl. 5/6; Bayern starts within Natur und Technik 7; BW and Niedersachsen use integrated science in Kl. 5/6). The KMK MSA standards (2024) set the Sek I contents (energy, electricity, mechanics, electromagnetic and ionising radiation). In the Oberstufe, mechanics in depth is taught in the Einführungsphase, and the KMK Abitur standards (2020) define fields, oscillations and waves, and quantum physics and matter at grundlegendes (gA, Grundkurs) and erhöhtes (eA, Leistungskurs) level; relativity and nuclear/particle physics are Länder extensions.

subjects.name: Informatik & Medienbildung
subjects.description: In Kl. 1–4 computing is integrated into Sachunterricht and Mathematik, and media education follows the KMK framework "Bildung in der digitalen Welt" (2016) in all subjects. A compulsory Informatik subject in Sek I now exists in most Länder but at different grades: NRW Kl. 5–6, Sachsen 7–10, Bayern in Natur und Technik 6–7 and for all pupils in Kl. 11, BW Kl. 7 (G9: Informatik und Medienbildung from Kl. 5), Niedersachsen 9–10, Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg 4 lessons within 7–10, MV and Thüringen combined with Medienbildung; Berlin, Brandenburg, Hessen, Rheinland-Pfalz, Sachsen-Anhalt and Bremen have no compulsory subject yet (status 2026). In the Oberstufe Informatik is an Abitur subject as Grundkurs (gA) and, in most Länder, Leistungskurs (eA); the KMK EPA Informatik (2004) and the GI standards (2008/2016/2025) are the national references.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Character Encoding: ASCII and Unicode
topics.description: Computers store text as numbers. Pupils encode and decode text with the ASCII table, explain why 7 or 8 bits are not enough for all the world's scripts and emojis, and how Unicode/UTF-8 solves this, including what goes wrong when encodings are mixed ("Mojibake" with ä, ö, ü).
evidence: Encodes a short word in ASCII as decimal and binary numbers and decodes it again
Explains how many different characters can be coded with 7, 8 and 16 bits
Explains why umlauts sometimes appear garbled in e-mails or files
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} receives a text where "Grüße" appears as "GrÃ¼ÃŸe", can they explain what went wrong with the encoding?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on binary numbers and bytes from Kl. 5–6
Codes need agreed meanings

osMatches.note: os: all data as numbers

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Raster and Vector Graphics
topics.description: Raster graphics store a colour value for every pixel; vector graphics store objects such as lines and circles with their attributes. Pupils compare scaling, file size and typical uses, and calculate the memory needed for an image from resolution and colour depth (RGB, 24 bit).
evidence: Explains why a photo becomes blocky when enlarged but a logo in SVG does not
Calculates the uncompressed file size of an image from resolution and colour depth
Chooses raster or vector format for given purposes and justifies the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must design a school logo that will be printed on both a pin and a banner, can they explain which kind of graphic to use and why?

prerequisites.reason: Colour depth and file size use bits and bytes
Builds on taking and editing photos

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats pixel and vector graphics in Natur und Technik 6; NRW in the Wahlpflichtfach 9/10.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Digitising Sound and Images
topics.description: Analogue signals such as sound are digitised by sampling at regular intervals and rounding each value to a fixed number of levels. Pupils explain sampling rate and bit depth, calculate data rates (e.g. CD audio) and judge the trade-off between quality and file size.
evidence: Explains sampling and quantisation with a sketch of an analogue signal
Calculates the data size of one minute of CD-quality audio
Explains how sampling rate and bit depth affect quality and file size
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records a voice memo, can they explain how the sound becomes numbers and what a higher sampling rate changes?

prerequisites.reason: Images are the first example of digitised data
Sampling needs sound as an oscillation with frequency and loudness

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Data Compression
topics.description: Pupils compress data losslessly with run-length encoding and Huffman coding, explain why lossy formats such as JPEG and MP3 can be much smaller by removing details humans hardly perceive, and judge which method suits text, images or music.
evidence: Compresses a simple black-and-white image with run-length encoding
Builds a Huffman code for a short text and calculates the saving
Explains the difference between lossless and lossy compression with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saves the same photo as PNG and as JPEG and sees very different file sizes, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Compression works on digitised data
Huffman codes replace fixed-length character codes

topics.laenderNotes: Optional in most Sek I plans; Niedersachsen includes compression in the Sek II Grundkurs.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Spreadsheets: Formulas and Cell References
topics.description: Pupils build spreadsheets in which cells contain values or formulas, copy formulas with relative references and fix them with absolute references ($), and understand the spreadsheet as a data-flow model in which results update automatically.
evidence: Writes formulas with cell references and basic functions (SUMME, MITTELWERT)
Explains the difference between relative and absolute references when copying a formula
Traces which cells change when an input value is altered
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plans the budget for a class trip in a spreadsheet, can they set it up so that changing the number of pupils updates all costs?

prerequisites.reason: Formulas are terms with variables
Spreadsheets are files to be saved and organised

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: functional relationships in tables
externalPrerequisites.reason: Spreadsheets model functions as tables

topics.laenderNotes: Sachsen teaches spreadsheets in Kl. 7, Saarland in 8, Bayern in Informatik 9 (NTG), Niedersachsen in 10; often also in Mathematik.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Analysing Data with Spreadsheets
topics.nameDe: Daten mit Tabellenkalkulation auswerten und darstellen
topics.description: Pupils use conditional functions (WENN), counting and lookup functions, sort and filter data, and choose suitable charts. They interpret the results and recognise misleading charts and the limits of correlations.
evidence: Uses WENN and ZÄHLENWENN to evaluate a data table
Sorts and filters a data set and creates a suitable chart with title and axis labels
Identifies a misleading chart or a correlation that is not a cause
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a table with the results of a school survey, can they analyse it in a spreadsheet and present a fair chart?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on formulas and references
Critical reading of charts from Kl. 5–6

osMatches.note: os tables, charts and graphs in science

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Database Tables, Records and Keys
topics.description: A relational database stores data in tables whose rows are records and columns attributes with fixed data types. Pupils compare databases with spreadsheets, choose a primary key and explain why redundancy in one big table causes problems.
evidence: Identifies records, attributes, data types and the primary key in a given table
Explains why a primary key must be unique and chooses one
Explains with an example why storing the same data twice leads to inconsistencies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the school library's lending list, can they explain how it would be stored in a database and what the key is?

prerequisites.reason: Tables are already known from spreadsheets
Distinguishing data and information

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern (Informatik 9) and Sachsen (Kl. 9) introduce databases in Sek I; NRW, Niedersachsen and BW only in the Oberstufe.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Querying a Database with SQL
topics.description: Pupils formulate queries in SQL to select columns, filter rows with conditions, sort results and count or average values (SELECT … FROM … WHERE … ORDER BY), and translate questions in everyday language into queries and back.
evidence: Writes SELECT queries with WHERE conditions combined by AND/OR
Sorts and aggregates results (ORDER BY, COUNT, AVG)
Explains in words what a given SQL query returns
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a database of the school's sports results, can they write a query that lists all 100 m times under 13 s sorted from fastest to slowest?

prerequisites.reason: Queries need the table structure
Conditions use comparison and logical operators

topics.laenderNotes: In Bayern and Sachsen in Kl. 9/10; NRW only in the Qualifikationsphase.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Entity-Relationship Modelling
topics.description: Pupils model a real-world situation (e.g. a cinema booking system) with entity types, attributes, relationship types and cardinalities (1:1, 1:n, n:m) in an ER diagram and judge whether the model fits the requirements.
evidence: Identifies entity types, attributes and relationships in a described situation
Draws an ER diagram with correct cardinalities
Assesses an ER model against the requirements and improves it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to design a database for a sports club with members, teams and trainers, can they draw a suitable ER diagram?

prerequisites.reason: ER models describe the tables of a database
Similar to class modelling

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern models cardinalities already in Informatik 10 (NTG); Niedersachsen places ER modelling at eA only.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: From ER Model to Relational Schema
topics.nameDe: Relationales Datenbankschema mit Primär- und Fremdschlüsseln
topics.description: Pupils transform an ER diagram into a relational schema: each entity type becomes a table, 1:n relationships become foreign keys and n:m relationships become separate linking tables; they implement the schema in a database system.
evidence: Converts entity types and 1:n relationships into tables with primary and foreign keys
Resolves an n:m relationship with a linking table
Implements a small schema in a database system and fills it with data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has an ER diagram for pupils and courses, can they turn it into tables and explain where the foreign keys go?

prerequisites.reason: The schema is derived from the ER model

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: SQL Queries across Several Tables
topics.nameDe: SQL: Verbund mehrerer Tabellen, Gruppierung und Aggregation
topics.description: Pupils combine tables with joins over foreign keys, group results (GROUP BY, HAVING), use aggregate functions and nested queries, and check that a query returns exactly the intended rows.
evidence: Writes a join of two or three tables via primary and foreign keys
Uses GROUP BY with aggregate functions to answer a question
Finds and corrects a query that returns too many rows because of a missing join condition
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must find out which teacher supervises the most AGs from a school database, can they write the SQL query with a join and grouping?

prerequisites.reason: Extends single-table queries
Joins follow foreign keys

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Normalisation and Anomalies
topics.description: Redundant tables cause insertion, update and deletion anomalies. Pupils check tables for the first three normal forms and decompose them so that every fact is stored once, keeping the data consistent.
evidence: Identifies insertion, update and deletion anomalies in a badly designed table
Brings a table into first, second and third normal form
Explains why normalisation improves consistency and when redundancy may be accepted
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a table where a customer's address is stored with every order, can they explain the problem and normalise the table?

prerequisites.reason: Normalisation refines a relational schema

topics.laenderNotes: Normal forms 1–3 are Grundkurs content in NRW; Bayern discusses anomalies in Kl. 10.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: First Steps in Text-Based Programming
topics.description: Pupils move from block-based to text-based programming (typically Python, sometimes Java): they write, run and correct small programs with input and output, read error messages, and distinguish syntax errors from logical errors.
evidence: Writes and runs a small program that reads input and prints a result
Uses an error message to find and fix a syntax error
Distinguishes a syntax error from a program that runs but gives a wrong result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} types a short Python program that asks for their age and prints the year they were born, can they fix the errors the computer reports?

prerequisites.reason: Variables are known from block-based programming
Builds on block-based programming from Kl. 3–6

osMatches.note: os first visual program

topics.laenderNotes: BW starts text-based programming in the IMP profile Kl. 9; NRW in the Wahlpflichtfach 9/10 or the Einführungsphase; Bayern pupils outside the NTG start in Kl. 11.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Data Types and Expressions
topics.description: Pupils use the basic data types integer, floating-point number, string and Boolean, evaluate arithmetic, comparison and logical expressions, convert between types and trace how assignments change variable values.
evidence: Chooses a suitable data type for a given value and explains the choice
Evaluates expressions with arithmetic, comparison and logical operators (and, or, not)
Traces the values of variables through a sequence of assignments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s program prints "1010" instead of 20 when adding two inputs, can they explain the type error and fix it?

prerequisites.reason: Types are used in text-based code

osMatches.note: os variables in programs

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Conditionals and Loops in Code
topics.nameDe: Kontrollstrukturen: Verzweigung und Schleife im Quelltext
topics.description: Pupils implement algorithms with conditionals (if/elif/else), counting loops (for) and conditional loops (while), nest them, and represent them in structograms. They choose the right loop type and avoid endless loops.
evidence: Implements an algorithm with nested conditionals and loops
Chooses between a counting loop and a conditional loop and justifies the choice
Converts between a structogram and code
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} programs a number-guessing game, can they use a loop and conditions so that it gives hints until the number is found?

prerequisites.reason: Control structures are written in text code
Loops are known from block coding
Conditions are known from block coding
Structograms are known from Kl. 5–6

osMatches.note: os nested loops in block code

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Functions with Parameters and Return Values
topics.description: Pupils decompose problems into subproblems and implement them as functions (methods) with parameters and return values, distinguish local and global variables, and reuse functions from libraries.
evidence: Writes a function with parameters that returns a value and calls it several times
Explains the difference between a parameter, an argument and a return value
Decomposes a larger task into functions and explains the benefit of modularisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to calculate the area of many different rooms in a program, can they write one function for it and use it repeatedly?

prerequisites.reason: Functions contain control structures

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: functions as input–output assignments
externalPrerequisites.reason: Programming functions mirror mathematical functions

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Lists and Arrays
topics.description: Pupils store many values of the same type in a list or array, access elements by index, traverse them with loops to sum, count or find the maximum, and avoid index errors. Two-dimensional arrays (grids, game boards) follow later.
evidence: Accesses and changes elements of a list by index, including the first and last
Traverses a list with a loop to compute a sum, average or maximum
Explains and fixes an "index out of range" error
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stores a week of temperature readings in a list, can they write a program that finds the warmest day?

prerequisites.reason: Lists are processed with loops

topics.laenderNotes: BW IMP profile Kl. 9, Bayern Informatik 10 (NTG), NRW Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Linear and Binary Search
topics.description: Pupils search lists linearly and, in sorted lists, by repeatedly halving the search range (binary search). They count comparisons and explain why binary search needs only about log₂(n) steps.
evidence: Implements a linear search that returns the position of a value or reports that it is missing
Carries out a binary search by hand and implements it
Compares the number of comparisons for both methods on a list of 1 000 elements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plays "guess my number between 1 and 1000", can they explain the best strategy and how many guesses it needs at most?

prerequisites.reason: Searching works on lists
Comparing algorithms was introduced in Kl. 5–6
Halving steps are counted with powers of two

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Simple Sorting Algorithms
topics.description: Pupils carry out, describe and implement simple sorting algorithms such as selection sort, insertion sort and bubble sort, trace them on example data and compare how many comparisons and swaps they need.
evidence: Sorts a set of cards by hand with selection sort and insertion sort and describes each step
Implements one simple sorting algorithm
Counts comparisons for a sorted and an unsorted list and explains the difference
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must sort the class list by birthday, can they describe a step-by-step method a computer could follow and estimate how much work it is?

prerequisites.reason: Sorting rearranges lists
Sorted lists enable binary search

topics.laenderNotes: BW (IMP 9, bubble sort), NRW Einführungsphase, Sachsen Kl. 10.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Systematic Testing and Debugging
topics.description: Pupils test programs systematically with planned test cases including boundary values and special cases, use a debugger or trace outputs to locate errors, and document what was tested.
evidence: Designs test cases including boundary values for a given function
Uses a debugger or print statements to locate a logical error
Documents tests and their results in a test table
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s grade-calculator program gives a wrong grade only for exactly 50 %, can they find the bug with suitable tests?

prerequisites.reason: Extends debugging from Kl. 3–6
Boundary values arise from conditions

osMatches.note: os testing and debugging for younger pupils

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Recursion
topics.description: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance until a base case is reached. Pupils trace recursive calls (e.g. factorial, Towers of Hanoi, fractal drawings), explain the call stack and compare recursive with iterative solutions.
evidence: Identifies base case and recursive step in a given function
Traces the calls of a recursive function with a call tree or stack diagram
Writes a recursive solution and an iterative one for the same problem and compares them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a recursive function for factorial, can they explain why it does not run forever and trace fact(4)?

prerequisites.reason: Recursion is a function calling itself

topics.laenderNotes: Grundkurs content in NRW, Bayern (Kl. 12) and Sachsen; the GI standards and Niedersachsen place recursion at eA only.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Divide and Conquer: Quicksort and Mergesort
topics.nameDe: Teile und Herrsche: Quicksort und Mergesort
topics.description: Pupils apply the divide-and-conquer strategy: split a problem, solve the parts recursively and combine the results. They trace and implement Quicksort or Mergesort and explain why these are much faster than simple sorting for large lists.
evidence: Traces Quicksort or Mergesort on a list of eight numbers
Implements a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm recursively
Explains why the number of steps grows like n·log n instead of n²
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must explain how a computer can sort a million names in a second, can they describe Mergesort and why it is fast?

prerequisites.reason: Divide and conquer is implemented recursively
Builds on simple sorting

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Efficiency and Big-O Notation
topics.description: Pupils estimate the running time and memory use of algorithms by counting operations as a function of input size, classify them with O-notation (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ)) and choose suitable algorithms for large data.
evidence: Counts the operations of a nested loop and states its order of growth
Orders algorithms by their complexity class and explains the effect of doubling the input
Measures running times experimentally and compares them with the prediction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} runs two sorting programs on 10 000 and then 20 000 numbers, can they predict and explain how the running times change?

prerequisites.reason: Sorting algorithms are the standard example
n·log n is shown with divide and conquer

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: growth of power, exponential and logarithmic functions
externalPrerequisites.reason: Complexity classes compare function growth

topics.laenderNotes: The NRW Grundkurs judges algorithms by the number of operations; comparing complexity classes is Leistungskurs content. The GI standards put efficiency comparison at eA.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Graphs and Shortest Paths
topics.description: Pupils model networks such as road maps or social networks as graphs with vertices and weighted edges, store them as adjacency matrices or lists, traverse them with breadth-first and depth-first search, and find shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm.
evidence: Models a real network as a graph and stores it as an adjacency matrix
Carries out breadth-first and depth-first search by hand
Applies Dijkstra's algorithm to find a shortest route
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a navigation app, can they explain with a graph how the shortest route can be found?

prerequisites.reason: Trees are special graphs; traversal ideas carry over
Breadth-first search uses a queue

topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs in NRW; Bayern treats graphs and Dijkstra in Informatik 11 (NTG).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Concurrency
topics.description: Several processes or threads can run at the same time and access shared resources. Pupils explain race conditions and deadlocks with everyday examples and code, and describe simple synchronisation (locks, monitors) that prevents them.
evidence: Explains a race condition with two processes updating the same account balance
Describes a deadlock with the dining philosophers or a traffic example
Explains how a lock or monitor ensures mutual exclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two people book the last concert ticket at the same moment online, can {{name}} explain what might go wrong in the software and how to prevent it?

prerequisites.reason: Processes run program code
Threads and monitors are often modelled as objects

topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs content in NRW; Bayern treats concurrency at gA in Kl. 12.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Objects, Classes, Attributes and Methods
topics.description: Pupils describe elements of documents and graphics (a text paragraph, a rectangle) as objects with attributes and values that belong to a class and can be changed by methods. They use object cards and class cards and dot notation such as rechteck1.füllfarbe = rot.
evidence: Describes a graphic object with its class, attributes and attribute values on an object card
Distinguishes a class (blueprint) from its objects (instances)
Uses dot notation to describe a method call that changes an attribute value
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a slide with several text boxes, can they describe each as an object of a class with attributes such as font size and colour?

prerequisites.reason: Documents are the first examples of objects
Vector graphics consist of objects with attributes

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces the object-oriented view in Natur und Technik 6, Sachsen in Kl. 7; NRW starts object orientation in the Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Implementing Classes
topics.description: Pupils implement classes in a programming language with attributes, a constructor and methods with parameters and return values, create objects, call methods on them and understand that variables of object types hold references.
evidence: Implements a class with attributes, a constructor and several methods
Creates several objects of a class and calls methods on them
Explains what happens when two variables refer to the same object
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes a class "Konto" with a deposit method, can they create two accounts and explain why changing one does not change the other?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the object/class concept
Methods are functions belonging to a class

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Informatik 9–10 (NTG) and 11 (all); NRW Einführungsphase; BW Kursstufe.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: UML Class Diagrams and Associations
topics.description: Pupils model a problem with UML class diagrams: classes with attributes, data types, methods and visibility, and associations with multiplicities and direction. They implement associations as references between objects.
evidence: Draws a class diagram with attributes, methods and visibility for a described situation
Models associations with multiplicities (e.g. 1 class has 0..* pupils)
Implements an association as an attribute that refers to another object or a list of objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to model a library with books, members and loans, can they draw a class diagram and explain the associations?

prerequisites.reason: Diagrams describe implementable classes

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Inheritance and Polymorphism
topics.description: Pupils model general and special classes (generalisation and specialisation), let subclasses inherit and override methods, explain polymorphism (the same call behaves differently for different subclasses) and use abstract classes as templates.
evidence: Models an inheritance hierarchy (e.g. vehicle – car – bike) in a class diagram
Overrides a method in a subclass and explains which version is called
Explains the purpose of an abstract class with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} programs a game with different enemy types that all move differently, can they explain how inheritance and polymorphism help?

prerequisites.reason: Inheritance is a relationship between classes

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern teaches inheritance already in Informatik 9 (NTG); Niedersachsen places class design with inheritance at eA.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Encapsulation and Information Hiding
topics.description: Objects hide their internal state behind methods: attributes are private and only accessed through public methods (getters, setters, operations that check validity). Pupils use documented class libraries through their interface only; eA courses add explicit interfaces as contracts.
evidence: Explains why attributes are usually private and accessed through methods
Writes a setter that rejects invalid values and so protects the object's state
Uses a documented class from a library without knowing its implementation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} programs a class "Konto", can they explain why the balance should not be changeable directly from outside?

prerequisites.reason: Visibility is part of implementing classes
Protected members matter with inheritance

topics.laenderNotes: Interfaces (Schnittstellen) are Leistungskurs content in NRW.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Stacks
topics.description: A stack stores elements by the last-in-first-out principle with the operations push, pop, top and isEmpty. Pupils use the abstract data type through its interface regardless of implementation, and apply stacks to undo functions, bracket checking and the call stack.
evidence: Traces a sequence of push and pop operations
Uses a stack to check whether brackets in an expression are balanced
Explains the difference between the interface of an abstract data type and its implementation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} presses "undo" several times in an editor, can they explain why a stack is the right data structure for it?

prerequisites.reason: Abstract data types are used as classes
Contrasts with static arrays

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Queues
topics.description: A queue stores elements by the first-in-first-out principle with enqueue, dequeue, front and isEmpty. Pupils use queues for waiting lines, print jobs and buffers, and compare them with stacks.
evidence: Traces a sequence of enqueue and dequeue operations
Chooses between stack and queue for a given application and justifies it
Uses a queue in a program simulating a waiting line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} models the queue at the school canteen in a program, can they explain which operations they need and in what order people are served?

prerequisites.reason: Introduced in contrast to stacks
Queues are used as classes

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Linked Lists
topics.description: A linked list consists of nodes that each hold a value and a reference to the next node, so it can grow and shrink at run time. Pupils insert, delete and traverse elements, draw the reference changes and compare linked lists with arrays.
evidence: Draws how references change when inserting a node into a linked list
Implements traversal and insertion for a linked list
Compares linked lists and arrays for access, insertion and memory use
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must insert a new name in the middle of a long list, can they explain why a linked list does this more easily than an array?

prerequisites.reason: Queues are often implemented with linked nodes
Nodes refer to other node objects

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Binary Trees and Traversals
topics.description: A binary tree consists of nodes with at most two children. Pupils describe root, leaves, depth and subtrees, traverse trees recursively in pre-, in- and post-order, and use trees for expressions, decision trees and file systems.
evidence: Names root, inner nodes, leaves and depth of a given tree
Gives the pre-order, in-order and post-order traversal of a tree
Implements a recursive traversal method
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws the expression (3 + 4) · 5 as a tree, can they show how a traversal evaluates it?

prerequisites.reason: Trees generalise linked nodes
Traversals are recursive
Decision trees were met in Kl. 5–6

topics.laenderNotes: Grundkurs in NRW and Bayern (Kl. 12); Niedersachsen places binary trees at eA.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Binary Search Trees
topics.description: In a binary search tree every left subtree holds smaller and every right subtree larger keys. Pupils insert and search elements, explain why search takes about log₂(n) steps in a balanced tree and n steps in a degenerate one, and compare with sorted lists.
evidence: Builds a binary search tree by inserting a sequence of keys
Searches a key and counts the comparisons
Explains why inserting sorted data produces a degenerate tree
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} inserts the numbers 1 to 7 in order into a binary search tree, can they explain what goes wrong and what a better order would be?

prerequisites.reason: A search tree is an ordered binary tree
Compared with binary search in lists

topics.laenderNotes: eA in Niedersachsen and in the GI standards; the EPA example task leaves binary search trees out of the Grundkurs version.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Modelling with Finite Automata
topics.description: Pupils model systems such as a vending machine, a traffic light or a combination lock as finite automata with states, inputs, transitions and outputs, draw state diagrams and transition tables, and check by simulation whether the automaton behaves as required.
evidence: Draws a state diagram with start state and labelled transitions for a described system
Translates a state diagram into a transition table and back
Tests an automaton with input sequences and finds a missing transition
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} designs the control of a parking-garage barrier, can they draw an automaton with its states and inputs?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on states and state diagrams from Kl. 3–6

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Wahlpflichtfach 9/10 and Sachsen Kl. 10; elsewhere first in the Oberstufe.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Types of Machine Learning
topics.description: Pupils distinguish supervised learning (labelled examples), unsupervised learning (finding clusters) and reinforcement learning (rewards), assign applications to them, and explain why a model is trained with training data and checked with separate test data.
evidence: Assigns applications (spam filter, customer groups, game AI) to the three types of learning
Trains a simple classifier with a tool and tests it with new data
Explains why training and test data must be kept separate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} trains an app to recognise their drawings of cats and dogs, can they explain what kind of learning this is and how to check whether it really works?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on learning from examples in Kl. 5–6
Decision trees are a simple learned model

osMatches.note: os machine-learning basics at age 7–9, without the three types of learning

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Wahlpflichtfach 9/10 and Einführungsphase, Sachsen Kl. 9, Bayern Kl. 11.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Data, Bias and Fairness in AI
topics.nameDe: Einfluss der Trainingsdaten: Verzerrung und Fairness
topics.description: The behaviour of a learned model depends on its training data. Pupils explain how unbalanced or biased data lead to unfair results (e.g. face recognition, job applications), distinguish correlation from causation, and suggest ways to detect and reduce bias.
evidence: Shows with an example how an unbalanced training set changes a classifier's results
Explains why a correlation found by a model need not be a cause
Suggests measures to check an AI system for unfair treatment of groups
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that an AI for job applications rejected more women, can they explain how this could happen through the training data?

prerequisites.reason: Bias arises in training
Builds on limits and risks of AI from Kl. 5–6

osMatches.note: os AI and fairness in decisions

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Generative AI and Language Models
topics.description: Generative AI systems produce text, images or sound. Pupils explain in simple terms that a language model predicts likely next words from patterns in huge training data, why it can produce convincing but false statements ("hallucinations"), how prompts shape the output, and how to use such tools responsibly in school (sources, copyright, data protection).
evidence: Explains the basic idea of next-word prediction in a language model
Checks an AI-generated answer against reliable sources and finds an error
States rules for responsible use of generative AI for homework, including marking AI help
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a chatbot for a presentation, can they explain why it may invent sources and how they check its answers?

prerequisites.reason: Language models are trained machine-learning models
Checking content builds on recognising fake news

osMatches.note: os deepfakes and AI-generated content
os AI mistakes and limitations

topics.laenderNotes: Explicit in the new NRW Sek II plan (generative KI, prompting); in most Länder treated in Informatik or across subjects under the KMK framework.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Classification and Clustering Methods
topics.description: Pupils explain and carry out a concrete supervised method (k-nearest neighbours or learning a decision tree) and an unsupervised one (k-means clustering) on small data sets, and discuss the effect of parameters such as k.
evidence: Classifies a new data point by hand with k-nearest neighbours
Carries out two iterations of k-means on a small set of points
Explains how the choice of k changes the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has data on the length and weight of fruits, can they use k-nearest neighbours to decide whether a new fruit is an apple or a pear?

prerequisites.reason: Concrete methods for the types of learning
Decision trees from Kl. 5–6 are now learned from data

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: distance between points in a coordinate system
externalPrerequisites.reason: k-NN and k-means use distances

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern teaches k-NN or decision trees in Informatik 11; NRW in the Grundkurs.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Artificial Neural Networks
topics.nameDe: Künstliche neuronale Netze: Neuronen, Schichten, Training
topics.description: Pupils describe artificial neurons with weighted inputs, a bias and an activation function, the layers of a network (input, hidden, output), forward propagation, and the basic idea of training by backpropagation, which adjusts the weights to reduce the error.
evidence: Calculates the output of a single perceptron for given inputs and weights
Describes the structure of a network with input, hidden and output layers
Explains in words how training adjusts weights to reduce the error
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a diagram of a neural network for recognising digits, can they explain what the layers do and how the network learns?

prerequisites.reason: Neural networks are one machine-learning method
Revisits the intuitive idea from Kl. 5–6 formally

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: weighted sums and functions; derivative as slope
externalPrerequisites.reason: Forward propagation uses weighted sums, training uses gradients

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Grundkurs (new plan 2027); Bayern Kl. 11 (perceptron) and 13 (AI, more at eA).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Evaluating AI Models
topics.nameDe: KI-Modelle bewerten: Über- und Unteranpassung, Präzision
topics.description: Pupils evaluate trained models with test data using a confusion matrix and measures such as accuracy, precision and specificity, recognise overfitting and underfitting, and judge whether a model is good enough for its purpose.
evidence: Fills in a confusion matrix and calculates accuracy and precision
Recognises overfitting from training and test results
Judges whether a model's error rate is acceptable for a given application (e.g. medical diagnosis)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a model detects 95 % of spam but also blocks 10 % of normal mail, can {{name}} evaluate it with suitable measures and say whether it is usable?

prerequisites.reason: Bias is one evaluation criterion
Models to evaluate come from classification methods

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: relative frequencies and conditional probability
externalPrerequisites.reason: Evaluation measures are conditional frequencies

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Finite Automata as Language Acceptors
topics.description: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) reads a word symbol by symbol and accepts it if it ends in an accepting state. Pupils define the alphabet, states, transition function and accepting states, determine the language a DFA accepts, develop DFAs for given languages (e.g. valid number formats) and meet non-deterministic automata.
evidence: Gives the formal components of a DFA and its transition table
Develops a DFA that accepts exactly the words of a described language
Determines whether given words are accepted and describes the accepted language
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must check whether user input is a valid German postcode, can they design a finite automaton that accepts exactly these strings?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on modelling with automata

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Grundkurs; Bayern Kl. 13; Niedersachsen gA (DFA, Mealy automata).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Formal Languages and Grammars
topics.description: Pupils describe formal languages with grammars (terminals, non-terminals, production rules, start symbol), derive words and draw derivation trees, use syntax diagrams or EBNF, and compare formal with natural languages, including syntax and semantics of programming and database languages.
evidence: Derives a word from a grammar and draws its derivation tree
Writes a grammar or syntax diagram for a simple language (e.g. e-mail addresses)
Explains the difference between syntax and semantics with a program or SQL example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given rules for valid licence plates, can they write them as a grammar and check whether a plate fits?

prerequisites.reason: Languages are introduced via automata and grammars together
Programming languages are formal languages
German sentence structure (Satzglieder) is the natural-language point of comparison

topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen treats regular and context-free grammars at eA.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Regular Languages and Their Limits
topics.nameDe: Reguläre Sprachen: Grammatik, Automat und Grenzen
topics.description: Regular grammars and finite automata describe the same class of languages. Pupils convert between them, and explain with examples such as correctly nested brackets or aⁿbⁿ why finite automata cannot recognise every language because they have no memory beyond their states. Leistungskurs courses add regular expressions.
evidence: Converts a regular grammar into a finite automaton and vice versa
Explains why no finite automaton accepts the language aⁿbⁿ
Judges whether a given language is regular
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tries to build a finite automaton that checks correctly nested brackets, can they explain why it cannot work for any depth?

prerequisites.reason: Regular languages are those accepted by finite automata
Regular grammars are a special type of grammar

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Pushdown Automata and Context-Free Languages
topics.description: A pushdown automaton adds a stack to a finite automaton and can therefore recognise context-free languages such as nested brackets or arithmetic expressions. Pupils develop pushdown automata, relate them to context-free grammars and to parsers in compilers.
evidence: Develops a pushdown automaton for a language such as aⁿbⁿ
Traces the stack contents while the automaton reads a word
Explains the link between context-free grammars, pushdown automata and parsing
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders how a compiler checks that all brackets in a program match, can they explain it with a pushdown automaton?

prerequisites.reason: Motivated by the limits of finite automata
The memory of the automaton is a stack

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Turing Machines
topics.description: A Turing machine reads and writes on an unbounded tape and is the standard model of what any computer can compute. Pupils program simple Turing machines (e.g. adding in unary, inverting bits) and explain the Church–Turing thesis.
evidence: Traces the run of a given Turing machine on an input tape
Develops a Turing machine for a simple task
Explains why the Turing machine is regarded as a universal model of computation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a Turing machine with a few states, can they simulate it on a tape and say what it computes?

prerequisites.reason: Turing machines extend automata with an unrestricted memory

topics.laenderNotes: Optional in Niedersachsen and not part of the new NRW plan; taught in Leistungskurs/eA courses in several Länder (e.g. Bayern 13 eA, Sachsen).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Limits of Computability: the Halting Problem
topics.description: Some problems cannot be solved by any algorithm. Pupils follow a plausibility argument (diagonalisation with a program that analyses itself) that no program can decide for all programs whether they halt, and discuss consequences such as the impossibility of a perfect virus scanner.
evidence: States the halting problem precisely
Reconstructs the contradiction argument with a self-applied program
Explains a practical consequence of undecidability
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to write a tool that detects every endless loop in any program, can they explain why this is impossible?

prerequisites.reason: The argument treats programs as functions on data
Automata are the first formal model of computation

topics.laenderNotes: The EPA name limits of computability for Grundkurs and Leistungskurs; Bayern treats the halting problem at gA as a plausibility argument and Sachsen in the Grundkurs. The GI standards place it at eA; the new NRW plan omits it.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Complexity Classes P and NP
topics.description: Some solvable problems have no known efficient algorithm. Pupils distinguish problems solvable in polynomial time from those where only checking a solution is fast (NP), discuss examples such as the travelling-salesman problem or SAT, and explain why the presumed hardness of factorising matters for cryptography.
evidence: Distinguishes polynomial and exponential running time with examples
Explains the difference between finding and checking a solution with an NP example
Explains why RSA relies on the presumed difficulty of factorisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plans the shortest round trip through 30 cities, can they explain why trying all routes is hopeless and what that says about the problem?

prerequisites.reason: Complexity classes generalise O-notation

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Networks: Clients, Servers and IP Addresses
topics.nameDe: Rechnernetze: Client, Server, Router und IP-Adressen
topics.description: Pupils describe local networks and the internet as networks of networks, explain the roles of clients, servers, switches and routers, and how data packets with IP addresses are forwarded hop by hop. They read a URL and explain what happens when a web page is requested.
evidence: Explains the roles of client, server and router when loading a web page
Explains why data are split into addressed packets that may take different routes
Reads the parts of a URL and finds the IP address of a device
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} opens a website from their phone, can they explain which devices the request passes and how the reply finds its way back?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on packets and protocols from Kl. 4–6

osMatches.note: os how the internet sends data

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Natur und Technik 7, BW Kl. 7, Sachsen Kl. 8.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: How the Web Works: DNS, HTTP and Layers
topics.description: Pupils explain how the Domain Name System translates names into IP addresses, how a browser and a web server communicate with HTTP(S), and how e-mail is sent and received, using a simple layer model in which each protocol has one task.
evidence: Explains the steps of resolving a domain name with DNS
Describes a request and response in HTTP and what HTTPS adds
Assigns protocols (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, TCP, IP) to the layers of a simple model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} types a web address into the browser, can they explain step by step how the page arrives, including DNS and HTTP?

prerequisites.reason: Protocols run on top of the network
HTTP transports HTML pages

topics.laenderNotes: Sachsen Kl. 9; BW IMP profile Kl. 10; Bayern Informatik 11.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Sensors, Actuators and Microcontrollers
topics.description: Pupils build and program small embedded systems (e.g. Calliope mini, Arduino) that read sensors (light, temperature, distance) and control actuators (LEDs, motors, buzzers), using the input–processing–output principle and threshold values.
evidence: Connects a sensor and an actuator to a microcontroller and reads sensor values
Programs a reaction to a threshold value (e.g. switch on a light when it gets dark)
Explains the system with the input–processing–output (EVA) model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants a plant to "call for water" when the soil is dry, can they plan and program a microcontroller with a sensor and an alarm?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on programming the Calliope mini
Uses the EVA principle

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Logic Gates and Circuits
topics.description: Pupils describe the logic gates AND, OR, NOT and XOR with truth tables and circuit symbols, combine them into circuits, simulate them, and build a half adder that adds two bits, showing how computers calculate with electricity.
evidence: Gives the truth tables of AND, OR, NOT and XOR
Builds and simulates a circuit for a given truth table
Builds a half adder and explains how it adds two binary digits
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants a lamp that lights when exactly one of two switches is on, can they design the logic circuit?

prerequisites.reason: Logic works on binary values
Boolean operators are known from programming

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Wahlpflichtfach 9/10 and BW IMP profile Kl. 10; in Bayern part of "how a computer works" in Kl. 12/13.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: How a Computer Works: von Neumann Architecture
topics.description: Pupils describe the von Neumann architecture (processor with control unit and arithmetic logic unit, registers, memory, bus), explain the fetch–decode–execute cycle and program a simple register machine or assembler model to see how high-level code is executed.
evidence: Names the components of a von Neumann computer and their tasks
Explains the fetch–decode–execute cycle with an example instruction
Writes a short program for a register machine (e.g. adding two numbers)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes x = a + b in Python, can they explain roughly what the processor does to execute it?

prerequisites.reason: The arithmetic unit is built from logic circuits
Builds on the parts of a computer from primary school

osMatches.note: os inside a computer at age 10–12

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats it in Kl. 12 (eA) and 13 (gA); register machines are eA in the GI standards.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Layered Network Protocols: TCP/IP
topics.description: Pupils explain the TCP/IP layer model (application, transport, internet, link layer), how IP routes packets, how TCP ensures complete and ordered delivery with ports, acknowledgements and retransmission, and why the layering makes networks flexible.
evidence: Assigns tasks and protocols to the layers of the TCP/IP model
Explains how TCP detects and repairs lost packets
Analyses a captured or simulated packet and identifies its layer headers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} streams a video while the connection is bad, can they explain what TCP does with lost packets and why a video call may use a different approach?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the simple layer idea from Sek I

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Informatik 11 and Sachsen Kl. 9 (TCP/IP); in the new NRW plan networks appear only in the Leistungskurs (protocols).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Designing Client–Server Protocols
topics.description: Pupils specify an application protocol (messages, states, error cases) for a client–server system such as a chat or a quiz server, implement it with sockets or a provided network library, and test it.
evidence: Specifies the messages and states of a simple protocol
Implements a client or server that follows the protocol
Tests the system with error cases (unknown command, lost connection)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a class quiz app with a server, can they define which messages client and server exchange and in what order?

prerequisites.reason: Application protocols build on TCP
Client and server are implemented as classes
Protocol states are modelled as an automaton

topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs content in the new NRW plan.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Symmetric Encryption and Its Weaknesses
topics.description: Pupils encrypt and decrypt with monoalphabetic substitution and the Vigenère cipher, break simple ciphers by frequency analysis, state Kerckhoffs' principle (security must lie in the key) and explain the key-exchange problem of symmetric methods.
evidence: Breaks a substitution cipher with frequency analysis of German letters
Encrypts and decrypts with the Vigenère cipher and explains why it resists simple frequency analysis
Explains the key-exchange problem of symmetric encryption
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} intercepts a long message encrypted by letter substitution, can they explain how to crack it without the key?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on comparing substitution and transposition
Caesar is the simplest substitution

topics.laenderNotes: BW Kl. 7 (Caesar, frequency analysis), Saarland Kl. 8, NRW Wahlpflichtfach; Niedersachsen Vigenère in Sek II.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Securing Data and Accounts
topics.description: Pupils apply the protection goals confidentiality, integrity and availability to their own data: they plan backups (3-2-1 rule, versioning), use two-factor authentication and password managers, install updates and recognise social-engineering attacks.
evidence: Explains confidentiality, integrity and availability with examples
Plans a backup strategy for their own files
Sets up two-factor authentication and explains why it protects even if a password is stolen
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s laptop were stolen tomorrow, can they explain which of their data would be lost and how they could have protected them?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on strong passwords
Builds on storage locations and backups

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Tracking, Profiling and Data Rights
topics.description: Pupils explain how websites and apps track users (cookies, device fingerprints, location data), how data brokers build profiles, and what rights the DSGVO gives them (information, correction, deletion, objection). They connect this to the German right to informational self-determination.
evidence: Explains how third-party cookies or app permissions allow cross-site tracking
Describes what a profile built from someone's data can reveal
Formulates a request for information (Auskunftsersuchen) under the DSGVO
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees adverts for shoes they only looked at on another site, can they explain how this happened and what they can do?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on DSGVO basics from Kl. 5–6

externalPrerequisites.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
externalPrerequisites.concept: fundamental rights in the Grundgesetz
externalPrerequisites.reason: Informational self-determination derives from the general right of personality

osMatches.note: os my digital footprint

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Datenschutz in Informatik 9 (NTG) and NuT 7; BW Kl. 7.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Asymmetric Encryption and RSA
topics.description: In asymmetric methods everyone has a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption, which solves the key-exchange problem. Pupils explain the principle, carry out RSA with small numbers (key generation, encryption, decryption with modular arithmetic) and explain hybrid encryption as used in HTTPS.
evidence: Explains the roles of public and private key with an example
Generates an RSA key pair with small primes and encrypts and decrypts a number
Explains why practical systems combine asymmetric and symmetric encryption
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to receive secret messages from people they have never met, can they explain how a public key makes this possible?

prerequisites.reason: Motivated by the key-exchange problem
RSA rests on prime numbers and factorisation

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Informatik 11, Sachsen Kl. 9 (asymmetric principle), NRW Grundkurs; RSA in detail is optional in Niedersachsen and often eA.

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Hash Functions, Signatures and Certificates
topics.description: Pupils explain how hash functions detect changes to data, how a digital signature (hash encrypted with the private key) proves authorship and integrity, and how certificates and certificate authorities let a browser trust a website's public key.
evidence: Explains why a small change to a file completely changes its hash
Describes the steps of signing and verifying a document
Explains what the browser checks when it shows the lock symbol for HTTPS
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} downloads software with a published checksum, can they explain how to check that the file was not tampered with?

prerequisites.reason: Signatures use the private key

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Informatik 11 (hashes, signatures); Niedersachsen gA (signatures).

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Data Protection Principles in Practice
topics.description: Pupils apply the core principles of data protection law – prohibition subject to permission (Verbot mit Erlaubnisvorbehalt), purpose limitation, data minimisation, transparency and necessity – to case studies such as video surveillance, learning platforms or health apps, and weigh privacy against security and convenience.
evidence: Explains the principle "Verbot mit Erlaubnisvorbehalt" and names legal bases for processing
Checks a case (e.g. a school app) against purpose limitation and data minimisation
Weighs privacy against security in a surveillance case and justifies a position
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s school wants to introduce video cameras in the corridors, can they assess the plan with the principles of data protection?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on data rights from Sek I

externalPrerequisites.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
externalPrerequisites.concept: tension between freedom and security in a democracy
externalPrerequisites.reason: The same conflict is discussed in politics lessons

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Software Licences and Open Source
topics.description: Pupils compare proprietary software, freeware, open-source licences (e.g. GPL, MIT) and Creative Commons licences, explain what each allows (use, change, share, sell), and judge licence choices for their own projects.
evidence: Explains the difference between freeware and open-source software
Reads a Creative Commons licence and states what is allowed
Chooses a licence for an own program or media product and justifies it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to use a free game asset in their school project and publish it, can they check the licence and say what they must do?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on copyright and citing sources

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Platforms, Power and Filter Bubbles
topics.description: Pupils analyse how large digital platforms gain power through network effects and lock-in, how recommendation algorithms optimise engagement and can create filter bubbles, and which interests (profit, participation, control) shape the design of these systems.
evidence: Explains network effects and lock-in with an example (messenger, social network)
Explains how a recommendation algorithm can narrow what someone sees
Discusses who benefits from a platform's design choices
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants their class to switch to a different messenger, can they explain why this is so hard?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on recommendation algorithms from Kl. 5–6

externalPrerequisites.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
externalPrerequisites.concept: market power, competition and monopolies
externalPrerequisites.reason: Economics explains market concentration

osMatches.note: os recommendation systems and filter bubbles at a younger age

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Digital Technology and Sustainability
topics.description: Pupils estimate the energy use of data centres, streaming and AI, examine the life cycle of devices (raw materials, production, e-waste), and discuss how informatics can both harm and support sustainability (e.g. smart grids, longer device use, efficient code).
evidence: Estimates the energy use of an hour of video streaming or of training a large AI model from given data
Describes the life cycle of a smartphone including raw materials and disposal
Names measures that make own IT use more sustainable
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that "the cloud" uses as much electricity as a country, can they explain where this energy goes and what they can do?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on computing in society from Kl. 5–6
Energy estimates use power, time and kWh

osMatches.note: os AI and the environment

topics.description: Pupils analyse how automation and AI change jobs and work processes, distinguish tasks that are easy or hard to automate, and assess opportunities and risks for individuals and society with examples from industry, medicine and administration.
evidence: Analyses which tasks of a given job are likely to be automated and why
Describes an example where automation created new kinds of work
Assesses social consequences of automation from several perspectives
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} thinks about a career, can they assess how AI might change that job in the next 20 years?

AI is a driver of current automation

topics.name: Ethics of Algorithmic Decisions

Applies at least two ethical perspectives to a case of algorithmic decision-making
Explains the risk-based approach of the EU AI Act with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether a self-driving car should be allowed to choose whom to protect in an accident, can they argue from different ethical positions?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on fairness issues of AI
Technical quality of models informs the ethical judgement

externalPrerequisites.subject: Religion & Ethik

externalPrerequisites.reason: Philosophy provides the ethical frameworks

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Building Web Pages with HTML and CSS
topics.nameDe: Webseiten mit HTML und CSS gestalten
topics.description: Pupils write web pages in HTML (headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images, tables), style them with CSS, and explain the separation of content and presentation and the hypertext structure of linked pages.
evidence: Writes a valid HTML page with headings, links and images
Changes the layout of several pages with one CSS file
Explains why content and presentation are kept separate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a small website for a school club, can they structure it in HTML and give all pages the same look with CSS?

prerequisites.reason: Structuring documents is known from word processing
Web pages are delivered over the internet

osMatches.note: os designing a user interface
