topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: How Search Engines Work
topics.description: Pupils explain how search engines crawl the web, build an index and rank results (link analysis in the spirit of PageRank, relevance, personalisation, paid ads), and use this knowledge to search more effectively and to judge why some results appear first.
evidence: Describes the steps crawling, indexing and ranking
Explains with a small link graph why pages with many incoming links rank higher
Distinguishes ads from organic results and explains the effect of personalisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets different search results than a friend for the same query, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on search strategies from Kl. 4–6
Ranking is not the same as reliability

topics.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
topics.name: Software Projects in Teams
topics.description: Pupils develop software in teams following a process model (e.g. waterfall or an agile model with user stories), agree interfaces and responsibilities, use version control, document their work and reflect on the process.
evidence: Splits a project into tasks with agreed interfaces and responsibilities
Uses version control to merge the work of several team members
Documents and reflects on the process and the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s group must build a game together, can they plan who does what, how the parts fit together and how they avoid overwriting each other's code?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on online collaboration
Teams divide the work along classes

osMatches.note: os writing user stories

topics.laenderNotes: Projects are explicit in Bayern (Informatik 10, 12) and BW (Kursstufe project management); the EPA expect teamwork for both course types.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Analysing Measurement Series
topics.description: Evaluate a measurement series by plotting it with axis labels and units, drawing a line of best fit (Ausgleichsgerade) and checking proportionality via constant quotients (Quotientengleichheit). From the slope the pupil reads off a physical constant such as a spring constant or a resistance.
evidence: Plots a measurement table as a graph with the dependent variable on the y-axis, labelled axes and units
Checks proportionality both by constant quotients and by a straight line through the origin
Determines a constant (e.g. D in F = D·s) from the slope of the line of best fit and states it with its unit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures how far a spring stretches for five different weights, can they draw the graph, decide whether stretch is proportional to force and work out the spring constant from it?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on recording measurements in tables and line graphs from Kl. 5–6
Proportional reasoning with the rule of three underlies the quotient test

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: proportional relationships and their graphs (Proportionalität, Ursprungsgerade)
externalPrerequisites.reason: The physics test for proportionality uses the mathematical definition

osMatches.note: os covers tables and graphs generally, not fitting lines or reading constants

topics.laenderNotes: Spreadsheet evaluation of data is explicitly required in NRW (IF7) and in the KMK 2024 standards (digital tools).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Measurement Uncertainty
topics.description: Every measurement has an uncertainty: pupils distinguish random scatter from systematic errors, repeat measurements and use the mean, estimate the reading uncertainty of an instrument, and give results with a sensible number of significant digits.
evidence: Distinguishes random errors (scatter of repeated readings) from systematic errors (e.g. zero offset of a scale)
Calculates the mean of repeated measurements and states a range such as t = (2,4 ± 0,1) s
Rounds a calculated result to a number of digits that matches the precision of the input values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} times a falling ball five times and gets slightly different values, can they explain why, give a mean with an uncertainty and suggest how to measure more precisely?

prerequisites.reason: Uncertainty is judged on evaluated measurement series
Uses the mean from Kl. 5–6 statistics
Extends basic measuring with instruments

osMatches.note: os covers repeating tests for reliability; German topic adds systematic error and significant digits

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Physical Models and Their Limits
topics.description: Physics explains with models (light ray, particle model, electron–ion-core model, field lines) that are made for a purpose. Pupils say which aspect of reality a model represents, use it to predict, and name where it fails, e.g. the ray model cannot explain diffraction.
evidence: Names for a given model (e.g. light ray) what it represents and what it leaves out
Uses a model to make a prediction and compares it with an experiment
Gives an example where a model fails and a better model is needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether light "really consists of rays", can they explain that the ray is a model, what it is good for and where it reaches its limits?

prerequisites.reason: The particle model from Kl. 6 is the first model pupils reflect on
The ray model of optics is a standard example

osMatches.note: os: science can be revised; German topic focuses on models

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Evaluating Technology with Criteria
topics.description: Pupils follow a structured evaluation procedure for a physics-related decision (e.g. heat pump or gas boiler, a phone charger, radiation protection): collect physics and non-physics criteria, weigh them, separate the factual judgement (Sachurteil) from the value judgement (Werturteil) and reflect on the decision.
evidence: Lists physical criteria (efficiency, power, risk) and non-physical criteria (cost, environment, comfort) for a decision
Weighs the criteria explicitly and justifies a decision
Separates statements of fact from value judgements in a discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has to advise their family whether a balcony solar module is worth it, can they list criteria, weigh them and explain which parts of their advice are facts and which are opinions?

prerequisites.reason: Uses the scientific way of reasoning from Kl. 5
Efficiency is a typical physical criterion

externalPrerequisites.subject: Politik und Wirtschaft
externalPrerequisites.concept: weighing arguments and forming a reasoned judgement (Urteilsbildung)
externalPrerequisites.reason: The same judgement-forming steps are taught in social studies

osMatches.note: os compares design solutions against criteria

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Planning Experiments and Error Analysis
topics.description: Plan an experiment from a theory-based hypothesis, choose measuring methods (incl. digital data logging and video analysis), linearise non-linear relations for evaluation and analyse how measurement uncertainties affect the result. This is the Oberstufe form of experimental work required for the Abitur.
evidence: Derives a testable hypothesis from theory and plans which quantities to vary, measure and keep constant
Linearises a relation (e.g. plots T² against l) to determine a constant from the slope with a regression tool
Estimates the uncertainty of a result from the input uncertainties and discusses whether the hypothesis is supported
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to find g with a pendulum, can they plan the measurement, evaluate it with a suitable linear plot and say how precise their value is?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on uncertainty concepts from Sek I
Linearisation extends the line-of-best-fit method

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: linear functions: slope and y-intercept
externalPrerequisites.reason: Linearised data are evaluated via slope and intercept

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Law of Reflection and Mirror Images
topics.nameDe: Reflexionsgesetz und Bild am ebenen Spiegel
topics.description: At a mirror the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (Einfallslot). With this law and straight-line propagation pupils construct where the virtual mirror image lies and explain its properties (same size, same distance, left–right swapped).
evidence: Measures angles of incidence and reflection from the normal and states the law
Constructs the mirror image of a point and of a simple object with rays
Explains why the image is virtual and appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stands 2 m in front of a mirror, can they draw where their image appears and explain with the law of reflection why it is there?

prerequisites.reason: Kl. 6 introduced directed reflection qualitatively
Angles must be measured and drawn
The image construction is a geometric reflection

osMatches.note: os topic also covers refraction

topics.laenderNotes: Taught in Kl. 8 in Bayern, 7/8 in BW, already in Kl. 5/6 in Niedersachsen and in Kl. 9/10 in Berlin-Brandenburg (Themenfeld Optische Instrumente).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Refraction of Light
topics.description: When light passes from air into water or glass it changes direction at the boundary: towards the normal when entering the optically denser medium, away from it when leaving. Pupils measure the angles and explain everyday effects such as the "broken" straw or a pool looking shallower.
evidence: Draws the refracted ray at an air–glass boundary bending towards the normal and at glass–air away from it
Measures pairs of angles of incidence and refraction and describes the qualitative relation
Explains with a ray diagram why a straw in water looks bent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a coin at the bottom of a glass of water, can they draw why it seems higher than it really is?

prerequisites.reason: Uses normals and angles like the law of reflection
Assumes straight-line propagation of light

osMatches.note: os combines reflection and refraction

topics.laenderNotes: Snell's law (Brechungsgesetz with sine) is quantitative in some Länder (e.g. BW Kl. 7/8 optional, Bayern Oberstufe); most Sek I plans keep refraction qualitative.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Total Internal Reflection
topics.description: Light going from glass or water into air is fully reflected above the critical angle (Grenzwinkel). Pupils explain how optical fibres (Glasfaserkabel), endoscopes and reflecting prisms use this effect.
evidence: States that total internal reflection only occurs from the optically denser into the less dense medium
Demonstrates the critical angle with a semicircular glass body and a light ray
Explains how light is guided through a bent optical fibre
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that the internet travels "as light through glass", can they explain why the light does not escape from the fibre?

prerequisites.reason: Total reflection is the limiting case of refraction

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Image Formation by Converging Lenses
topics.description: Converging lenses focus parallel light in the focal point (Brennpunkt); diverging lenses spread it. Pupils construct images with the three principal rays (Parallel-, Mittelpunkt-, Brennpunktstrahl), describe how image size and position change with object distance, and use the lens equation 1/f = 1/g + 1/b where the Land requires it.
evidence: Identifies converging and diverging lenses by shape and by their effect on parallel light
Constructs the image of an object with the principal rays and states whether it is real, inverted, enlarged or reduced
Predicts how the image changes when the object moves towards the focal point and checks this on the optical bench
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} moves a candle closer to a magnifying lens, can they predict with a ray diagram what happens to the image on the screen?

prerequisites.reason: Lenses work by refraction at two curved surfaces

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: rearranging formulas with fractions
externalPrerequisites.reason: Needed where the lens equation is used quantitatively

osMatches.note: os ray diagrams and images; German topic centres on converging lenses

topics.laenderNotes: BW treats lenses qualitatively; Berlin-Brandenburg uses the lens equation in Kl. 9/10; Niedersachsen introduces lenses already in Kl. 5/6. NRW stresses construction and simulation.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Eye and Vision Defects
topics.description: The eye forms a real, inverted image on the retina; the lens changes its focal length to focus (Akkommodation). Pupils explain short-sightedness and long-sightedness and why diverging or converging spectacle lenses correct them.
evidence: Labels the optical parts of the eye and explains where the image is formed
Explains accommodation as a change of the lens's focal length
Draws why a short-sighted eye needs a diverging lens and a long-sighted eye a converging lens
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s friend can read but not see the board clearly, can they explain what is wrong with the image in the eye and which glasses help?

prerequisites.reason: The eye is an imaging system with a converging lens

externalPrerequisites.subject: Biologie
externalPrerequisites.concept: structure of the human eye (Netzhaut, Linse, Pupille)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Biology describes the anatomy of the eye

osMatches.note: os describes the eye biologically, without vision defects or lens optics

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Optical Instruments
topics.description: Pupils explain how a camera, magnifying glass, microscope and telescope use one or two lenses to form images, and judge what these instruments made possible in research and everyday life.
evidence: Explains how a camera or projector produces a sharp real image on a sensor or screen
Describes the magnifying glass as a lens used inside its focal length
Explains the two-lens principle of microscope or telescope (objective and eyepiece)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks through a telescope, can they explain why two lenses are needed and what each does?

prerequisites.reason: All instruments are combinations of lenses

osMatches.note: os covers telescopes only, without the lens principle

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Colour: Spectrum and Colour Mixing
topics.description: A prism splits white light into the spectrum because each colour is refracted differently (Dispersion); infrared and ultraviolet lie beyond the visible ends. Coloured objects absorb part of the spectrum. Pupils distinguish additive colour mixing of light (RGB, screens) from subtractive mixing of pigments (CMYK, printing).
evidence: Explains the spectrum behind a prism and places infrared and ultraviolet next to it
Explains the colour of a red T-shirt in white and in green light by absorption and reflection
Predicts additive mixtures (red + green = yellow) and explains why screens use RGB but printers CMYK
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} zooms into a phone screen showing yellow, can they explain why they only see red and green dots?

prerequisites.reason: Dispersion is colour-dependent refraction
Absorption and reflection explain body colours

osMatches.note: os white light and colour; German topic adds RGB/CMYK colour models

topics.laenderNotes: Colours and colour mixing appear already in Natur und Technik 7 in Bayern; BW places the prism in 7/8.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.description: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum, which ranges from radio and mobile-phone radiation via microwaves, infrared, visible and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays. Pupils order the ranges by wavelength and energy, name uses and risks, and know that sensors (thermal cameras, UV meters) detect what our senses cannot.
evidence: Orders radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV and X-ray radiation by wavelength
Names a use and a health consideration for at least four ranges (e.g. Wi-Fi, IR camera, sunburn, X-ray)
Explains that thermal cameras show infrared radiation emitted by warm bodies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that mobile-phone radiation and X-rays are "both radiation", can they place both in the spectrum and explain why only one is ionising?

prerequisites.reason: Extends the visible spectrum to the full electromagnetic spectrum

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Earth's Radiation Budget and Greenhouse Effect
topics.description: Earth absorbs short-wave solar radiation and emits long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit part of the infrared, which raises the surface temperature (natural greenhouse effect); more CO₂ strengthens this (anthropogenic effect). Pupils also discuss albedo (Rückstrahlvermögen) and tipping elements.
evidence: Draws a simple radiation balance with incoming solar and outgoing infrared radiation
Explains the difference between the natural and the anthropogenic greenhouse effect
Explains with albedo why melting sea ice amplifies warming (feedback)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears someone say "the greenhouse effect is bad", can they explain why without any greenhouse effect Earth would be frozen, and what changes when CO₂ increases?

prerequisites.reason: Needs the distinction between visible and infrared radiation
Heat transport by radiation was introduced in Kl. 6

externalPrerequisites.subject: Erdkunde
externalPrerequisites.concept: climate change: causes and consequences
externalPrerequisites.reason: Geography treats climate change from the human-geography side

externalPrerequisites.subject: Chemie
externalPrerequisites.concept: carbon dioxide as a combustion product
externalPrerequisites.reason: Chemistry explains where CO₂ comes from

osMatches.note: os greenhouse gas science; German topic adds radiation budget and albedo

topics.laenderNotes: New binding content in the KMK 2024 standards (Klimaphysik); older Länder plans place it in Erdkunde or as an optional physics context.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Solar System and Gravity
topics.description: Pupils describe the structure of the solar system (Sun, planets, moons, comets, asteroid belt), explain that gravity holds it together and keeps planets on their orbits, and explain weightlessness in the ISS as free fall rather than missing gravity.
evidence: Orders the planets and describes differences between rocky planets and gas giants
Explains that gravity between masses keeps moons and planets on their orbits
Explains why astronauts in the ISS float although gravity there is almost as strong as on the ground
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told that "there is no gravity in space", can they correct this using the example of the ISS and the Moon?

prerequisites.reason: Weight as the effect of gravity is the starting point
Erdkunde Kl. 5 introduced Earth's orbit around the Sun and the seasons

osMatches.note: os universal gravitation is more quantitative

topics.laenderNotes: An obligatory Inhaltsfeld in NRW (IF6 Sterne und Weltall); in most other Länder astronomy is optional or part of Erdkunde.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Moon Phases and Eclipses
topics.description: Using straight-line propagation of light and a Sun–Earth–Moon model, pupils explain the lunar phases as changing views of the half-lit Moon and explain solar and lunar eclipses as shadows, including why eclipses are rare.
evidence: Explains a phase (e.g. waxing crescent) with a sketch of Sun, Earth and Moon positions
Explains solar and lunar eclipses with umbra and penumbra
Explains why there is not an eclipse every month (tilted lunar orbit)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a half moon in the evening sky, can they show with a ball and a lamp where Sun, Earth and Moon are?

prerequisites.reason: Eclipses are shadows; umbra and penumbra were introduced in Kl. 6
Uses the Sun–Earth–Moon system

osMatches.note: os covers moon phases only

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Stars, Light-Years and Stellar Evolution
topics.description: Stars are suns at enormous distances measured in light-years. Pupils describe the main stages of a star's life (from gas cloud via main sequence to red giant and white dwarf, or supernova for massive stars) and how spectra and parallax tell us about stars.
evidence: Explains the light-year as a distance and compares distances to the Moon, the Sun and the nearest star
Describes the life cycle of a Sun-like star and of a massive star
Names spectra and parallax as ways astronomers learn about composition and distance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that the light of a star took 600 years to reach us, can they explain what this means and that the star might have changed since?

prerequisites.reason: Stars are introduced by comparison with our Sun

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Speed and Uniform Motion
topics.description: Speed is distance per time (v = s/t). Pupils calculate speeds, convert between m/s and km/h, distinguish average from instantaneous speed, and read and draw position–time graphs for uniform motion, where the slope is the speed.
evidence: Calculates speed, distance or time with v = s/t and converts km/h into m/s (factor 3.6)
Distinguishes the average speed of a journey from the speed shown on a speedometer
Reads speeds from the slope of a position–time graph and draws the graph for a described journey
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cycles 6 km to school in 20 minutes, can they work out their average speed in km/h and m/s and sketch the position–time graph?

prerequisites.reason: Speed calculations are proportional reasoning
Builds on measuring and drawing line graphs
Graphs are drawn in a coordinate system

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: proportional functions and their graphs
externalPrerequisites.reason: A uniform motion is a proportional function of time

osMatches.note: os covers reading distance–time graphs

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Acceleration and Free Fall
topics.description: Acceleration is the change of velocity per time (a = Δv/Δt). Pupils describe uniformly accelerated motion with velocity–time graphs, use v = a·t and s = ½·a·t², and explain free fall as motion with g ≈ 9.81 m/s² that is independent of mass when air resistance is negligible.
evidence: Calculates an acceleration from a change of speed and the time taken
Reads acceleration as the slope and distance as the area in a velocity–time graph
Explains with the vacuum tube experiment why a feather and a coin fall equally fast without air
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a stone into a well and hears it hit the water after 2 s, can they estimate how deep the well is and what assumptions they made?

prerequisites.reason: Acceleration is defined as a change of velocity

osMatches.note: os covers gravity and falling objects qualitatively

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern and Niedersachsen introduce acceleration in Kl. 7/8; BW (3.3.5) fixes it in Kl. 10, Berlin-Brandenburg in 9/10; NRW and NI deepen it in the Einführungsphase.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Forces, Deformation and Hooke's Law
topics.description: Forces are recognised by their effects: they deform bodies or change their motion. Force is measured in newton with a spring balance (Federkraftmesser), which works because the extension of a spring is proportional to the force (Hooke's law, F = D·s) within its elastic range. Forces are drawn as arrows with point of application, direction and length.
evidence: Names the two kinds of effects of forces with examples (deformation, change of speed or direction)
Draws a force as an arrow to scale and measures forces with a spring balance
Measures the extension of a spring and decides whether Hooke's law holds, including its limit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hangs more and more weights on a rubber band and on a steel spring, can they explain which one follows Hooke's law and how a spring balance uses this?

prerequisites.reason: Hooke's law is found by evaluating a measurement series
Builds on measuring with instruments

osMatches.note: os covers moments, pressure and Hooke's law together

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mass and Weight
topics.description: Mass (kg) is a property of a body that measures its inertia and does not depend on location; weight (N) is the gravitational force on it, F_G = m·g, with the local gravitational field strength (Ortsfaktor) g ≈ 9.81 N/kg on Earth and 1.62 N/kg on the Moon.
evidence: Explains why an astronaut's mass stays the same on the Moon while the weight changes
Calculates weights with F_G = m·g for Earth and other celestial bodies
Measures mass with a balance and weight with a spring balance and relates the two
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that a rover "weighs 900 kg", can they explain what is wrong with the wording and calculate its weight on Earth and on Mars?

prerequisites.reason: Weight is a force measured in newton

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Adding and Resolving Forces
topics.description: Forces are vectors. Pupils add forces acting along a line and at an angle with a scale drawing (Kräfteparallelogramm) to find the resultant, and resolve a force into components, e.g. the weight on an inclined plane into a downhill and a normal component.
evidence: Adds two forces in the same and opposite directions and states the resultant
Constructs the resultant of two forces at an angle with a force parallelogram to scale
Resolves the weight of a sledge on a slope into components parallel and perpendicular to the slope
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two friends pull a boat with ropes at an angle, can {{name}} construct the total force on the boat with a scale drawing?

prerequisites.reason: Forces as arrows are the basis for vector addition
Scale drawings need angles

osMatches.note: os resultant forces along a line

topics.laenderNotes: BW treats forces at an angle only in Kl. 10 (3.3.5); Bayern adds velocity arrows in Kl. 8.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Inertia: Newton's First Law
topics.description: A body stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed unless a net force acts on it. Pupils use the principle of inertia to explain everyday situations such as seat belts, a tablecloth trick or why a spacecraft needs no engine to keep moving.
evidence: States the principle of inertia and corrects the idea that motion needs a force
Explains with inertia why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes
Identifies whether the forces on a body are balanced from its state of motion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} says "the ball stops because its force is used up", can they explain with the principle of inertia what really slows it down?

prerequisites.reason: Needs the concept of force and of net force

osMatches.note: os combines Newton's first and second laws

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Action–Reaction and Balanced Forces
topics.description: Forces always come in pairs: if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force (actio = reactio). Pupils distinguish such interaction pairs, which act on two different bodies, from two balanced forces acting on the same body.
evidence: Names the partner force for a given force (e.g. foot pushes ground – ground pushes foot)
Explains why interaction forces do not cancel each other out
Distinguishes the equilibrium of weight and table force on a book from the interaction pair book–Earth
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} jumps off a small boat onto the jetty, can they explain why the boat moves backwards?

prerequisites.reason: Needs forces as arrows
Equilibrium links to the principle of inertia

osMatches.note: os balanced and unbalanced forces

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Newton's Second Law
topics.description: A net force accelerates a body: F = m·a. Pupils calculate accelerations, forces and braking distances, explain why heavier vehicles need more force for the same acceleration, and connect the law to the change of momentum F·Δt = m·Δv.
evidence: Calculates the acceleration of a body from net force and mass
Determines the net force from all forces on a body before applying F = m·a
Explains with F = m·a why a fully loaded lorry brakes less quickly than an empty one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a car of 1 200 kg brakes with a force of 6 000 N, can {{name}} work out the deceleration and how long it takes to stop from 50 km/h?

prerequisites.reason: The law links force and acceleration
Mass is the second quantity in the law
The first law is the special case F = 0

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: rearranging equations with several variables
externalPrerequisites.reason: Formulas are solved for different quantities

osMatches.note: os covers first and second laws together at a more qualitative level

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces it in Kl. 8 as F·Δt = m·Δv; BW places it in Kl. 10; NRW and Niedersachsen formalise it in the Einführungsphase (Kl. 11).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Friction
topics.description: Friction opposes relative motion. Pupils distinguish static, sliding and rolling friction, use F_R = μ·F_N with tabulated coefficients, and discuss where friction is wanted (tyres, brakes) and where it is reduced (bearings, lubrication).
evidence: Distinguishes static, sliding and rolling friction with examples
Measures the sliding friction of a block with a spring balance and calculates μ
Explains why ABS keeps tyres rolling instead of sliding to shorten the braking distance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pulls a box across a floor, can they explain why it is harder to start it moving than to keep it moving?
