Body current depends on voltage and resistance

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Magnetic Fields of Currents and Electromagnets
topics.description: A current produces a magnetic field (Oersted). Pupils draw the field lines around a straight wire and a coil using the right-hand rule, explain why an iron core strengthens a coil, and describe applications of electromagnets such as relays, door openers and scrap cranes.
evidence: Draws the circular field lines around a wire and determines their direction
Explains the field of a coil as the superposition of the fields of its windings and compares it with a bar magnet
Explains how a relay uses an electromagnet to switch a second circuit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} winds a wire around a nail and connects a battery, can they explain why the nail now picks up paper clips and how to make it stronger?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on magnetic fields and field lines from Kl. 6
Field strength grows with current

topics.laenderNotes: BW (3.2.4) and Niedersachsen teach electromagnets in 7/8; Bayern in Kl. 10 (Elektromagnetismus).

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Force on a Current and the Electric Motor
topics.description: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (Lorentz force) perpendicular to current and field. Pupils determine its direction with a hand rule (e.g. conductor swing), and explain how a DC motor uses this force with a commutator to keep rotating.
evidence: Predicts the direction of the force on a conductor swing with a hand rule
Explains the role of the commutator in a DC motor
Names ways to make a motor turn faster or reverse its direction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} takes apart a small toy motor, can they point out magnet, coil and commutator and explain why it turns?

prerequisites.reason: The motor uses the magnetic field of a coil

osMatches.note: os motors and the motor effect

topics.laenderNotes: BW teaches the motor in 7/8, Bayern in Kl. 10, Berlin-Brandenburg in 9/10.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electromagnetic Induction
topics.description: A voltage is induced in a coil whenever the magnetic field through it changes, e.g. by moving a magnet or switching a current. The induced voltage is larger for faster changes, more windings and stronger fields. Pupils name applications such as induction hobs, wireless charging and bicycle dynamos.
evidence: Shows with a coil, magnet and voltmeter that only a change of the field induces a voltage
Names the factors that increase the induced voltage
Explains an everyday application such as wireless phone charging with induction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pushes a magnet into a coil and holds it still, can they explain when the meter shows a voltage and when not?

prerequisites.reason: Induction is the reverse of the magnetic effect of currents
The result of induction is a voltage

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Generator and Alternating Voltage
topics.description: A generator turns a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet in a coil), which continuously changes the field and induces an alternating voltage. Pupils describe the sine-shaped voltage, its period and frequency (50 Hz in the European grid) and compare generator and motor as reverse processes.
evidence: Explains why a rotating coil produces a voltage that changes direction
Reads period, frequency and peak voltage from an oscilloscope or data-logger graph
Compares the energy conversion in a generator with that in a motor
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} turns the crank of a hand generator connected to a lamp, can they explain why it gets harder to turn when the lamp lights up?

prerequisites.reason: The generator is an application of induction
Generator and motor share their structure

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Transformer and Power Transmission
topics.description: A transformer changes alternating voltages: U₁/U₂ ≈ N₁/N₂ for an ideal transformer. Pupils explain why it only works with AC and why electrical energy is transmitted at high voltage: for the same power the current is smaller and the energy lost as heat in the lines (P = I²·R) drops.
evidence: Calculates output voltage or number of windings with the transformer equation
Explains why a transformer does not work with direct current
Explains with P = U·I and P_loss = I²·R why transmission lines use 380 kV
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees high-voltage power lines, can they explain why the electricity is not simply sent at 230 V?

prerequisites.reason: The transformer works by induction
Transmission losses are calculated with power

topics.laenderNotes: Niedersachsen treats motor, generator and transformer only as "black boxes" in Sek I.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Semiconductors: Diode, LED and Solar Cell
topics.description: Semiconductors conduct better when warm or illuminated and can be doped. Pupils describe the diode as a one-way valve for current, record its characteristic curve, and explain LEDs and solar cells as semiconductor devices that convert between electrical energy and light.
evidence: Shows that a diode conducts in one direction only and draws its characteristic curve
Explains why an LED needs a series resistor
Explains the energy conversion in a solar cell and how its power depends on the light
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} connects an LED the wrong way round and it stays dark, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Characteristic curves are compared with ohmic resistors
Conduction is explained with charge carriers

topics.laenderNotes: Part of BW 3.3.2 and Niedersachsen Elektrik II (9/10); NTG profile in Bayern Kl. 10; not required in NRW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Atomic Nuclei and Isotopes
topics.description: The atomic nucleus consists of protons and neutrons (nucleons) and is tiny compared with the atom (Rutherford's scattering experiment). Pupils read nuclide notation, explain isotopes as nuclei with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and use the chart of nuclides (Nuklidkarte).
evidence: Explains what Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed about the atom
Reads mass number, atomic number and neutron number from nuclide notation such as ¹⁴C
Explains what isotopes are and finds them on the chart of nuclides
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads about "carbon-12" and "carbon-14", can they explain what is the same and what is different about these atoms?

prerequisites.reason: Needs charges in the atom

externalPrerequisites.subject: Chemie
externalPrerequisites.concept: atomic structure with nucleus and electron shells (Kern-Hülle-Modell, Schalenmodell)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Chemistry introduces the atom model first

osMatches.note: os atoms, elements and compounds (chemistry view)

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiation
topics.description: Unstable nuclei decay and emit alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (electrons) or gamma radiation (high-energy photons). Pupils compare range, penetrating power, ionising effect and deflection in fields, write simple decay equations, and compare them with X-rays.
evidence: Describes what each type of radiation consists of and how it is produced in the nucleus
Compares the penetrating power of α, β and γ radiation (paper, aluminium, lead)
Writes a decay equation for an α or β decay and checks mass and charge numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} must choose a shield for an alpha and for a gamma source, can they explain what material and thickness are needed?

prerequisites.reason: Radiation comes from changes in the nucleus

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Detecting Radiation and Activity
topics.description: Ionising radiation can be detected with a Geiger–Müller counter, a cloud chamber or a film badge. Pupils measure count rates, subtract the natural background (Nullrate), and explain the activity of a source in becquerel (decays per second).
evidence: Explains how a Geiger–Müller counter detects radiation
Measures the background count and corrects a measured count rate for it
Explains the unit becquerel and why activity is not the same as danger
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} switches on a Geiger counter in the classroom and it ticks without any source, can they explain why and how to deal with it in a measurement?

prerequisites.reason: Detectors respond to the ionising effect of radiation

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life
topics.description: Radioactive decay is random for a single nucleus but statistically predictable for many: after each half-life half of the remaining nuclei have decayed. Pupils model decay with dice, read half-lives from decay curves and apply them to radiocarbon dating and to the storage time of radioactive waste.
evidence: Explains why the decay of a single nucleus cannot be predicted but that of many nuclei can
Determines the half-life from a measured or simulated decay curve
Calculates the remaining fraction after several half-lives and applies it to C-14 dating
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a substance has a half-life of 30 years, can they explain how much of it is left after 90 years and whether it is then "gone"?

prerequisites.reason: Decay curves are measured as count rates
Halving repeatedly uses powers

osMatches.note: os radiometric dating of rocks applies half-life

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Radiation Dose and Protection
topics.description: Ionising radiation can damage cells and DNA. Pupils compare the effective dose (sievert) from natural sources, medical imaging and flights, judge limits critically, and apply the protection rules distance, shielding, short exposure time and avoiding incorporation.
evidence: Explains how ionising radiation can damage living cells
Compares typical doses (natural background in Germany, X-ray, CT, flight) in mSv
Applies the rules of radiation protection to a concrete situation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs a CT scan and is worried about radiation, can they compare its dose with the natural yearly dose and weigh benefit against risk?

prerequisites.reason: Effects depend on type and energy of the radiation

externalPrerequisites.subject: Biologie
externalPrerequisites.concept: DNA and mutations
externalPrerequisites.reason: Radiation damage is explained with DNA changes

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Uses of Ionising Radiation
topics.nameDe: Medizinische und technische Anwendungen ionisierender Strahlung
topics.description: Pupils explain how X-ray imaging, CT, radioactive tracers (e.g. PET, thyroid scans), radiotherapy and sterilisation of food or instruments use ionising radiation, and weigh benefits and risks for patients and staff.
evidence: Explains how an X-ray image is formed by different absorption in tissues and bones
Explains why tracers for medical diagnosis need a short half-life
Weighs benefits and risks of an application with physical and medical arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a broken arm X-rayed, can they explain why bones show up white and why the staff leave the room?

prerequisites.reason: Uses are judged against radiation risks
Tracer choice depends on half-life

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Nuclear Fission and Nuclear Power
topics.description: Heavy nuclei such as U-235 can split after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy and further neutrons. Pupils explain the controlled chain reaction in a reactor (moderator, control rods, cooling), its risks and the problem of long-term storage of waste, and assess information from different interest groups, including the German nuclear phase-out (2023) and the search for a repository.
evidence: Describes a fission reaction and explains why a chain reaction can occur
Explains the roles of moderator, control rods and coolant in a reactor
Compares arguments of different groups on nuclear power and waste storage and states a reasoned position
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that Germany switched off its last nuclear plants in 2023 while other countries build new ones, can they explain how a reactor works and weigh the arguments?

prerequisites.reason: Fission is a change of nuclei
Fission products are radioactive
Uses the structured evaluation procedure

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Nuclear Fusion and the Sun
topics.description: Light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes fuse into helium and release energy; this powers the Sun and other stars. Pupils explain why fusion needs extremely high temperatures and describe the idea and challenges of fusion reactors (e.g. ITER, Wendelstein 7-X).
evidence: Describes the fusion of hydrogen to helium in the Sun
Explains why fusion requires temperatures of millions of degrees
Compares fusion and fission as energy sources by fuel, waste and technical maturity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that fusion is "the energy of the stars", can they explain what happens in the Sun and why we cannot simply copy it yet?

prerequisites.reason: Fusion is a change of nuclei
Stars shine because of fusion

osMatches.note: os where elements come from (stellar fusion)

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Quarks and Leptons
topics.description: Protons and neutrons are made of up and down quarks; electrons and neutrinos are leptons. Pupils describe matter as built from a few elementary particles and explain beta decay as a quark changing its type.
evidence: Explains the quark composition of proton (uud) and neutron (udd) and checks the charges
Names electron and neutrino as leptons
Explains β⁻ decay as the change of a down quark into an up quark
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked what a proton is made of, can they answer with quarks and show that the charges add up?

prerequisites.reason: Quarks are the building blocks of nucleons
Beta decay is reinterpreted with quarks

topics.laenderNotes: Quarks are part of Sek I in Bayern (Kl. 10) and BW (9/10); NRW introduces them in the Grundkurs; other Länder do not require them.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Law of Radioactive Decay
topics.description: The number of undecayed nuclei falls exponentially: N(t) = N₀·e^(−λt), with decay constant λ = ln 2 / T½, and the activity is A = λ·N. Pupils fit measured decay data, determine half-lives (e.g. radon or a protactinium generator), and use the law for dating.
evidence: Derives the relation λ = ln 2 / T½ and converts between them
Determines the half-life from measured count rates with a logarithmic plot or regression
Calculates the age of a sample from its remaining activity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the count rate of a short-lived source every 20 s, can they determine its half-life with the decay law?

prerequisites.reason: Formalises the half-life concept from Sek I

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: exponential functions with base e and the natural logarithm
externalPrerequisites.reason: The decay law is an e-function

topics.laenderNotes: Only a suggested extension in the KMK standards. Taught at both levels in Bayern (13) and Niedersachsen; in NRW only in the Leistungskurs; not in the Berlin-Brandenburg Q-phase.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
topics.description: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons; the mass defect corresponds to the binding energy via E = m·c². The binding energy per nucleon curve explains why fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei both release energy.
evidence: Calculates the mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus from tabulated masses
Explains the shape of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve and its maximum near iron
Explains with the curve why both fission and fusion release energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the binding-energy curve, can they explain why uranium is split but hydrogen is fused to gain energy?

prerequisites.reason: Explains the energy release of fission
Explains the energy release of fusion

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: powers of ten and scientific notation
externalPrerequisites.reason: Nuclear masses are given in u and kg with powers of ten

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Kl. 13 at both levels; NRW Leistungskurs (E = mc² also in the Grundkurs); not in Niedersachsen and Berlin-Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Standard Model of Particle Physics
topics.description: All known matter consists of six quarks and six leptons; three fundamental interactions (strong, weak, electromagnetic) are mediated by exchange particles (gluons, W/Z bosons, photons), and the Higgs field gives particles mass. Pupils describe beta decay with the weak interaction and know how particle accelerators such as those at CERN test the model.
evidence: Sorts elementary particles into quarks, leptons and exchange bosons
Assigns the four interactions to their exchange particles and examples
Describes β⁻ decay as a weak process with a W⁻ boson in a simple diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears about the discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN, can they explain where it fits into the Standard Model?

prerequisites.reason: Extends the quark–lepton picture from Sek I
The strong interaction holds the nucleus together

topics.laenderNotes: Not binding in the KMK standards; Bayern treats it with beta decay in Kl. 13, BW as an elective deepening topic in the Leistungsfach, NRW touches quarks in the Grundkurs.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Field Concept
topics.description: A field describes how space around a charge, magnet or mass is changed so that forces act at a distance. Pupils compare electric, magnetic and gravitational fields, use field lines as a model (direction, density, sources) and discuss what the model can and cannot show.
evidence: Draws the field lines of a point charge, a dipole, a plate capacitor and a bar magnet
Explains what direction and density of field lines mean
Compares the electric, magnetic and gravitational field by sources and kind of force
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how the Sun "knows" where the Earth is, can they explain the field idea and its limits?

prerequisites.reason: Electric fields start from charges
Magnetic fields of currents were introduced in Sek I
The gravitational field is the third example

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electric Field Strength
topics.description: The electric field strength is the force per charge on a test charge, E = F/q, in N/C = V/m. In the homogeneous field of a plate capacitor E = U/d. Pupils measure forces on charged bodies and use the Millikan experiment to show that charge is quantised in multiples of the elementary charge e.
evidence: Calculates field strength, force or charge with E = F/q
Uses E = U/d for a plate capacitor and explains why the field inside is homogeneous
Explains how the Millikan experiment shows that charge comes in multiples of e = 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sets up a plate capacitor with 2 000 V across 4 cm, can they calculate the field strength and the force on a charged oil droplet?

prerequisites.reason: Field strength quantifies the field concept
Force balance and motion of droplets

topics.laenderNotes: The Millikan experiment is part of the NRW Grundkurs and the Berlin-Brandenburg Q1; Bayern introduces the elementary charge already in Kl. 9.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Capacitor and Capacitance
topics.description: A capacitor stores charge and electrical energy. Its capacitance is C = Q/U; for a plate capacitor C = ε₀·ε_r·A/d. The stored energy is E = ½·C·U². Pupils measure the charge with a charge amplifier or by integrating a discharge current and discuss capacitors as short-term energy stores (camera flash, supercaps).
evidence: Calculates capacitance, charge or voltage with C = Q/U and for a plate capacitor
Explains how a dielectric and the plate geometry change the capacitance
Calculates the energy stored in a capacitor and compares it with a battery
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the capacitor in a camera flash, can they work out how much energy it stores and why the flash is so bright for such a short time?

prerequisites.reason: The plate capacitor is the standard homogeneous field
Energy storage links to electrical energy

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Charging and Discharging a Capacitor
topics.description: When a capacitor discharges through a resistor, current and voltage fall exponentially: U(t) = U₀·e^(−t/RC). Pupils record charging and discharging curves with a data logger, determine the time constant τ = R·C, and get the charge as the area under the I–t curve.
evidence: Records a discharge curve and determines the time constant τ = R·C
Describes the charging and discharging curves with exponential functions
Determines the stored charge from the area under the current–time graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures how the voltage of a discharging capacitor falls over time, can they find R·C from the graph and predict when only 1 % is left?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on capacitance
Discharge current is limited by a resistor

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: exponential functions with base e
externalPrerequisites.reason: The curves are e-functions

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: integral as area under a curve
externalPrerequisites.reason: Charge is the area under the I–t graph

topics.laenderNotes: Grundkurs content in NRW, Bayern and Niedersachsen; only Leistungsfach/Leistungskurs in BW and Berlin-Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Potential
topics.description: The force between two point charges is F = q₁·q₂/(4π·ε₀·r²). Pupils describe the radial field of a point charge, define the electric potential as energy per charge relative to a zero level, and interpret voltage as a potential difference, including equipotential lines.
evidence: Calculates the force between two charges with Coulomb's law and compares it with gravity
Defines the potential and draws equipotential lines for a point charge and a plate capacitor
Explains voltage as a potential difference and calculates the work on a charge moved in the field
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares the electric and gravitational force between two electrons, can they calculate both and explain the result?

prerequisites.reason: Coulomb's law gives the field strength of a point charge
Same mathematical form as the law of gravitation

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: integration of power functions
externalPrerequisites.reason: The potential of a radial field is found by integration

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Magnetic Flux Density
topics.description: The strength of a magnetic field is described by the flux density B, defined by the force on a current-carrying conductor, F = I·l·B (unit tesla). Pupils measure B with a current balance or a Hall probe and investigate the field of a long coil, B = μ₀·μ_r·N·I/l.
evidence: Determines B from the force on a conductor in a current balance
Investigates how the field inside a long coil depends on current, number of turns and length
Uses a Hall probe or app sensor to measure magnetic flux density
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses the magnetometer in a phone near a coil, can they explain what B measures and how it depends on the current?

prerequisites.reason: B quantifies the magnetic field
Uses the force on a conductor from Sek I

topics.laenderNotes: The Hall effect itself is eA/Leistungskurs content in NRW, Niedersachsen, Berlin-Brandenburg and BW; Bayern treats it at both levels.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Lorentz Force on Moving Charges
topics.description: A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences the Lorentz force F = q·v·B, perpendicular to velocity and field. Pupils explain qualitatively why charged particles move on circular or helical paths (fine-beam tube, aurora, Earth's magnetic shield) and determine directions with a hand rule.
evidence: Calculates the Lorentz force on an electron moving perpendicular to B
Determines the direction of deflection of electrons and positive ions with a hand rule
Explains qualitatively why the path in a homogeneous B-field is a circle and how the aurora forms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a picture of the northern lights, can they explain with the Lorentz force why they appear near the poles?

prerequisites.reason: The force depends on B
Generalises the force on a conductor to single charges

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Accelerating Charges in Electric Fields
topics.description: A charge accelerated through a voltage U gains kinetic energy q·U = ½·m·v². Pupils calculate electron speeds in an electron gun, use the electron-volt as energy unit, and describe qualitatively the parabolic path in a transverse field.
evidence: Calculates the final speed of an electron after acceleration through a given voltage
Converts energies between joule and electron-volt
Explains qualitatively the path of an electron entering a transverse electric field
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an electron in an old TV tube is accelerated by 20 kV, can {{name}} calculate its speed and check whether it is still well below the speed of light?

prerequisites.reason: Charges are accelerated by the field
Uses energy conservation with kinetic energy

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Trajectories of Charged Particles
topics.nameDe: Bahnen geladener Teilchen: e/m, Wien-Filter, Massenspektrometer
topics.description: Pupils calculate the paths of charged particles in homogeneous fields: parabolas in transverse electric fields and circles in magnetic fields with r = m·v/(q·B). They determine the specific charge e/m with the fine-beam tube (Fadenstrahlrohr) and explain velocity filters and mass spectrometers as applications.
evidence: Derives the radius of the circular path from Lorentz force = centripetal force
Determines e/m of the electron from fine-beam tube data
Explains how a Wien filter selects one speed and how a mass spectrometer separates isotopes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the radius of the glowing electron circle in a fine-beam tube, can they calculate the specific charge of the electron?

prerequisites.reason: The Lorentz force acts as centripetal force
Particles are first accelerated in an electric field
Uses the centripetal force
The deflection in a transverse field is analogous to a horizontal throw

topics.laenderNotes: The KMK standards put quantitative trajectories at eA. NRW (Grundkurs) and Bayern (both levels) nevertheless determine e/m with the fine-beam tube, and Bayern and Niedersachsen teach the Wien filter at both levels.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Rule
topics.description: The induced voltage equals the rate of change of the magnetic flux Φ = B·A through the coil times the number of turns: U = −N·ΔΦ/Δt (eA: −N·dΦ/dt). The minus sign expresses Lenz's rule: the induced current opposes its cause, as in eddy-current brakes and the jumping ring.
evidence: Calculates the induced voltage for a changing B-field and for a changing area
Explains with Lenz's rule why a magnet falls slowly through a copper tube
Interprets a measured U(t) graph as the derivative of a Φ(t) graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} drops a magnet through a copper pipe and it falls slowly, can they explain why with Lenz's rule?

prerequisites.reason: Flux is defined with B
Formalises the qualitative induction of Sek I

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: derivative as instantaneous rate of change
externalPrerequisites.reason: The law relates voltage to the rate of change of flux

topics.laenderNotes: The KMK standards require the differential form only at eA; gA courses work with difference quotients.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Self-Induction and Inductance
topics.description: A coil opposes changes of its own current because the changing field induces a voltage in it: U = −L·dI/dt. Pupils explain delayed switching-on and voltage spikes when switching off, calculate the inductance of a long coil and the energy stored in its magnetic field.
evidence: Explains why a lamp in series with a coil lights up with a delay
Explains the high voltage when switching off a coil (e.g. in an ignition coil)
Calculates the inductance of a long coil and the energy E = ½·L·I²
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a spark when unplugging a motor, can they explain it with self-induction?

prerequisites.reason: Self-induction applies the law of induction to the coil itself

topics.laenderNotes: eA/Leistungskurs in NRW and Niedersachsen; Bayern teaches it at both levels; BW has one example in the Basisfach.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Harmonic Oscillations
topics.description: An oscillation is harmonic when the restoring force is proportional to the displacement; then the displacement follows a sine function y(t) = ŷ·sin(ω·t). Pupils describe amplitude, period, frequency and phase, record oscillations with sensors and link the motion to the projection of a circular motion.
evidence: Reads amplitude, period and frequency from a recorded oscillation graph
Explains why a linear restoring force leads to a harmonic oscillation
Writes the equation y(t) for a given oscillation and relates ω to the frequency
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records the motion of a mass on a spring with a phone sensor, can they read off its period and write down the equation of motion?

prerequisites.reason: The restoring force follows Hooke's law
Motion follows from F = m·a
Angular frequency links to circular motion

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: sine and cosine functions and their parameters
externalPrerequisites.reason: Oscillations are described with sine functions

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern starts oscillations and waves in Kl. 11; NRW and Niedersachsen in the Qualifikationsphase.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Spring and Simple Pendulums
topics.description: The period of a spring pendulum is T = 2π·√(m/D), that of a simple pendulum for small angles T = 2π·√(l/g). Pupils test the formulas experimentally, explain why the period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass, and analyse the energy changes during the oscillation.
evidence: Calculates the period of a spring or simple pendulum
Checks experimentally how the period depends on mass, spring constant or length
Describes the conversion between kinetic and potential (or elastic) energy during one period
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants a pendulum clock to tick once per second, can they calculate how long the pendulum must be?

prerequisites.reason: Pendulums are the standard harmonic oscillators
Formulas are tested with linearised data

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The LC Oscillating Circuit
topics.description: In a circuit of capacitor and coil, energy swings between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the coil. Pupils describe the analogy with a spring pendulum, use Thomson's formula T = 2π·√(L·C), and explain why real circuits are damped.
evidence: Describes the energy exchange between capacitor and coil over one period
Calculates the frequency of an LC circuit with Thomson's formula
Draws the analogy between LC circuit and spring pendulum quantity by quantity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tunes an old radio, can they explain that they are changing the frequency of an oscillating circuit?

prerequisites.reason: The circuit is an electrical harmonic oscillator
Energy is stored in the capacitor
The coil acts by induction

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Damped and Forced Oscillations, Resonance
topics.description: Real oscillations lose energy (damping). A periodically driven oscillator responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches its natural frequency (resonance). Pupils compare mechanical and electrical oscillators energetically, record resonance curves and discuss wanted and dangerous resonance (radio tuning, bridges, buildings in earthquakes).
evidence: Describes the exponential decay of amplitude in a damped oscillation
Records a resonance curve and explains how damping changes it
Explains a case of resonance catastrophe and how engineers prevent it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a video of the Tacoma Narrows bridge, can they explain resonance and why soldiers break step on bridges?

prerequisites.reason: Damping and resonance are studied on pendulums
Electrical resonance is the basis of tuning

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: exponential functions with base e
externalPrerequisites.reason: The amplitude decays exponentially

topics.laenderNotes: Berlin-Brandenburg treats damping and resonance qualitatively already in Kl. 9/10.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Mechanical Waves
topics.nameDe: Mechanische Wellen: Kenngrößen, Transversal- und Longitudinalwellen
topics.description: A wave transports energy but not matter by coupled oscillators. Pupils use wavelength, frequency and propagation speed (c = λ·f), distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves and explain that only transverse waves can be polarised, with examples from ropes, sound and light (polarising filters).
evidence: Calculates wavelength, frequency or speed with c = λ·f
Distinguishes transverse and longitudinal waves and gives an example of each
Explains polarisation with two polarising filters and why sound cannot be polarised
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at an LCD screen through polarising sunglasses and turns their head, can they explain what they see?

prerequisites.reason: A wave is a propagating oscillation
Sound was introduced as a wave phenomenon in Kl. 6

osMatches.note: os wave properties and types at age 11–12

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Huygens' Principle and Interference
topics.description: Every point of a wavefront is the source of an elementary wave (Huygens). Pupils explain diffraction at gaps and obstacles, and interference of two coherent sources with path differences: constructive for Δs = k·λ and destructive for Δs = (2k+1)·λ/2, demonstrated in a ripple tank and with sound.
evidence: Explains diffraction behind a narrow gap with Huygens' principle
Determines constructive and destructive interference from the path difference
Explains the interference pattern of two loudspeakers or two ripple-tank sources
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} walks between two loudspeakers playing the same tone, can they explain why it gets quieter and louder at certain places?

prerequisites.reason: Interference is the superposition of waves

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Double Slit and Diffraction Grating
topics.description: Light passing a double slit or a grating produces interference maxima at sin α = k·λ/g. Pupils measure the wavelength of laser light, explain the spectra of white light behind a grating, and use a grating spectrometer to compare light sources; this shows the wave nature of light.
evidence: Derives the condition for maxima at a double slit or grating from the path difference
Determines the wavelength of a laser from measured maxima positions
Explains the spectrum of white light behind a grating and why red is diffracted most
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shines a laser pointer through a CD acting as a grating, can they measure the pattern and calculate the laser's wavelength?

prerequisites.reason: Applies the interference condition to light
Explains spectra known from the prism

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: trigonometry: sine and tangent in right-angled triangles
externalPrerequisites.reason: Angles of maxima are calculated with sine and tangent

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern starts double-slit interference in Kl. 11; the grating and X-ray diffraction follow in Kl. 12.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Standing Waves
topics.description: Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions form a standing wave with nodes and antinodes. Pupils explain the possible wavelengths on a string fixed at both ends and in air columns (L = k·λ/2) and apply this to musical instruments and microwave ovens.
evidence: Explains how a standing wave forms by reflection and superposition
Calculates the possible frequencies of a guitar string from its length and wave speed
Measures the wavelength of a standing wave (e.g. microwave or sound tube) from node distances
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} presses a guitar string at half its length, can they explain why the tone is one octave higher?

prerequisites.reason: Standing waves are a superposition
Pitch and frequency from Kl. 6
Octaves and intervals are known from music lessons

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Single-Slit Diffraction
topics.description: Light passing a single slit produces a broad central maximum and minima at sin α = k·λ/b. Pupils derive the minima by dividing the slit into zones, explain the narrowing of the pattern for wider slits, and relate it to the resolution limit of optical instruments.
evidence: Derives the condition for minima at a single slit
Determines a slit width from the measured pattern
Explains why the double-slit pattern is modulated by the single-slit envelope
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a laser beam through a narrowing slit, can they explain why the light spreads out more instead of less?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on interference conditions for light

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Interferometers
topics.description: An interferometer splits a light beam, sends the parts along different paths and recombines them; tiny path changes shift the interference pattern. Pupils explain the Michelson interferometer, measure small lengths or refractive indices, and know its role in the Michelson–Morley experiment and gravitational-wave detectors.
evidence: Explains the beam paths in a Michelson interferometer
Calculates a length change from the number of shifted fringes
Explains how LIGO uses an interferometer to detect gravitational waves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that LIGO measures length changes smaller than a proton, can they explain the principle of the interferometer?

prerequisites.reason: Uses interference of light

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.description: An oscillating circuit opened up into an antenna (Hertzian dipole) emits electromagnetic waves: coupled electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light. Pupils explain how radio, mobile phones and microwaves use them, place them in the spectrum and show reflection, polarisation and interference with microwaves.
evidence: Describes the dipole as an open oscillating circuit and the fields it emits
Calculates the wavelength of a radio or Wi-Fi signal from its frequency
Demonstrates polarisation or interference of microwaves and explains the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a Wi-Fi router's antennas, can they estimate the wavelength used and explain how the signal is produced?

prerequisites.reason: The dipole is an opened oscillating circuit
Uses wave quantities
Builds on the spectrum from Sek I

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats electromagnetic waves at both levels in Kl. 12; the Hertzian dipole is Leistungskurs/Leistungsfach content in NRW and BW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Photoelectric Effect
topics.description: Light can release electrons from a metal only above a threshold frequency, however bright it is; the electrons' maximum energy grows linearly with frequency. Pupils explain why the wave model fails here and how Einstein's photon idea, h·f = W_A + E_kin, explains the observations.
evidence: Describes the Hallwachs experiment and the key observations of the photoelectric effect
Explains which observations contradict the wave model of light
Uses Einstein's equation to calculate the work function or the maximum electron energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that red light cannot discharge a zinc plate however bright it is, but weak UV light can, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Electron energies are measured with a counter-voltage
The wave model of light is the contrast

topics.laenderNotes: Grundkurs content in NRW, BW and Berlin-Brandenburg; Bayern and Niedersachsen treat the photoelectric effect only at eA and determine h at gA with LEDs or the X-ray spectrum.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Photons and Planck's Constant
topics.description: Light energy is transferred in quanta (photons) with E = h·f and momentum p = h/λ. Pupils determine h, for example from the onset voltages of LEDs of different colours or with the counter-field method, and calculate photon energies and numbers for lasers and lamps.
evidence: Calculates the energy of a photon of given wavelength in J and eV
Determines Planck's constant from LED onset voltages or counter-field data
Estimates how many photons per second a 1 mW laser pointer emits
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures at which voltage red, green and blue LEDs start to glow, can they use the data to determine Planck's constant?

prerequisites.reason: Wavelengths are measured with a grating
The photoelectric effect motivates the photon idea
The LED method uses semiconductor diodes

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Electron Diffraction and the de Broglie Wavelength
topics.description: Electrons passing through a graphite foil produce diffraction rings like waves. Their de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. Pupils determine the wavelength from the ring diameters, check λ ∝ 1/√U, and explain why electron microscopes resolve smaller details than light microscopes.
evidence: Explains the rings in the electron diffraction tube as wave interference
Calculates the de Broglie wavelength of electrons for a given accelerating voltage
Explains why the resolution of an electron microscope is better than that of a light microscope
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} raises the accelerating voltage in an electron diffraction tube, can they predict and explain how the rings change?

prerequisites.reason: Electron momentum follows from the accelerating voltage
The pattern is explained with interference
λ = h/p uses momentum

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Quantum Objects at the Double Slit
topics.description: Single photons or electrons arrive at random points on a screen, yet many of them build up an interference pattern. Pupils explain the basic features of quantum objects: stochastic predictability, superposition, the determined probability distribution, and complementarity (which-path information destroys interference), e.g. with a Mach–Zehnder interferometer.
evidence: Describes how an interference pattern builds up from single detection events
Explains why the place where a single photon is detected cannot be predicted while the pattern can
Explains with a which-path experiment that path information and interference exclude each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches a simulation where single electrons hit a screen behind a double slit, can they explain what is random and what is predictable?

prerequisites.reason: Electrons show wave behaviour
Light shows particle behaviour

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: probability and relative frequency
externalPrerequisites.reason: Quantum predictions are probabilities

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Probability Interpretation of the Wave Function
topics.description: In quantum mechanics a wave function ψ describes the state; the square of its absolute value gives the probability density of finding the object at a place (Born's interpretation). Pupils interpret |ψ|² qualitatively for the double slit and simple bound states.
evidence: States that |ψ|² gives a probability density, not a "smeared-out" particle
Relates the brightness of an interference pattern to |ψ|²
Sketches |ψ|² for a simple situation and reads off where the object is likely found
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a graph of |ψ|² for an electron, can they explain what it tells us and what it does not?

prerequisites.reason: Formalises the stochastic behaviour of quantum objects

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Uncertainty Principle
topics.description: Position and momentum of a quantum object cannot both be sharply defined: Δx·Δp ≥ h/(4π). Pupils derive the relation qualitatively from single-slit diffraction, estimate its consequences for electrons in atoms, and distinguish it from measurement error.
evidence: Derives Δx·Δp ≈ h from single-slit diffraction of electrons
Estimates the minimum momentum uncertainty of an electron confined to an atom
Explains why the relation is a property of quantum objects, not of imperfect instruments
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that "Heisenberg says we disturb things when we measure", can they explain what the uncertainty principle really states?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the wave behaviour of quantum objects
The derivation uses single-slit diffraction

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Quantum Worldview
topics.description: Pupils reflect on how quantum physics changes the concepts of reality, locality, causality and determinism (Copenhagen interpretation, entanglement) and how modern quantum technologies (quantum cryptography, quantum computers) use these features. In eA courses the coincidence method shows that single photons exist.
evidence: Explains in what sense quantum physics is not deterministic for single events
Describes entanglement in simple terms and why it does not allow faster-than-light messages
Discusses an application of quantum technology and its significance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked whether "the Moon is there when nobody looks", can they discuss what quantum physics says about reality?

prerequisites.reason: Reflection needs the experimental features of quantum objects

externalPrerequisites.subject: Religion & Ethik
externalPrerequisites.concept: philosophical concepts of determinism and causality
externalPrerequisites.reason: Philosophy discusses determinism and causality in general

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Line Spectra and Energy Levels
topics.description: Atoms emit and absorb light only at specific wavelengths because their electrons can only have discrete energies. Pupils explain emission and absorption spectra (including Fraunhofer lines), draw energy-level diagrams, and calculate wavelengths of transitions, e.g. the Balmer series of hydrogen.
evidence: Explains emission and absorption lines with transitions between energy levels
Calculates the wavelength of a transition from an energy-level diagram
Explains how the Fraunhofer lines reveal the elements in the Sun
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a street lamp through a grating and sees only a few coloured lines, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Each line corresponds to photons of one energy
Spectra are measured with a grating

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces photons, spectra and energy levels already in Kl. 9 (Atome); in BW energy levels appear only in the Basisfach with astro focus.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The Franck–Hertz Experiment
topics.description: In the Franck–Hertz experiment electrons collide with mercury or neon atoms; the current drops at regular voltage intervals because atoms only absorb fixed energy portions. Pupils interpret the characteristic curve and relate the 4.9 V spacing to the light emitted.
evidence: Describes the setup and explains the periodic drops in the current
Determines the excitation energy from the measured curve
Relates the excitation energy to the wavelength of the emitted UV or visible light
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a Franck–Hertz curve with minima every 4.9 V, can they explain what this says about mercury atoms?

prerequisites.reason: Confirms discrete energy levels by collisions
Electrons gain energy e·U in the field

topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs only in Berlin-Brandenburg.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: X-Ray Spectra
topics.description: An X-ray tube produces a continuous bremsstrahlung spectrum with a sharp short-wavelength limit (Duane–Hunt law, λ_min = h·c/(e·U)) and characteristic lines of the anode material. Pupils explain both parts and determine h from the cut-off; eA courses add Bragg reflection on crystals.
evidence: Explains how bremsstrahlung and characteristic lines are produced in an X-ray tube
Uses the Duane–Hunt law to calculate the limiting wavelength or Planck's constant
Explains why the characteristic lines identify the anode material
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} increases the voltage of an X-ray tube, can they predict how the spectrum changes and why?

prerequisites.reason: Electrons are accelerated in the tube
The cut-off follows from E = h·f

topics.laenderNotes: Not named in the KMK standards; Grundkurs in NRW, both levels in Bayern, eA/Leistungskurs in Niedersachsen and Berlin-Brandenburg, absent in BW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: The One-Dimensional Potential Well
topics.description: An electron confined between infinitely high walls can only form standing de Broglie waves, so its energy is quantised: E_n = n²·h²/(8·m·L²). Pupils derive the energy levels, sketch the wave functions and probability densities, apply the model to dye molecules and discuss its limits for real atoms.
evidence: Derives the allowed energies from the standing-wave condition
Sketches ψ and |ψ|² for the first three states
Uses the model to estimate the colour of a dye molecule and names its limits
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} models an electron in a molecule as a particle in a box, can they explain why its energy can only take certain values?

prerequisites.reason: Uses the de Broglie wavelength
Energy quantisation follows from standing waves
Interprets |ψ|²

topics.laenderNotes: eA in the KMK standards, NRW and Berlin-Brandenburg; Bayern and Niedersachsen teach it at both levels; absent in BW.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: A Quantum Model of the Atom
topics.description: Pupils explain why Bohr's model of fixed orbits fails and describe the atom with a quantum model in which electrons occupy states with certain energies and probability distributions (orbitals). They relate the model to line spectra and to the structure of the periodic table (eA: Pauli principle).
evidence: Names successes and failures of Bohr's atomic model
Describes an orbital as a region of high probability density, not an orbit
Explains qualitatively how the quantum model explains discrete energy levels
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s chemistry book shows electron shells and the physics book shows orbitals, can they explain how the two pictures are related?

prerequisites.reason: The model must explain discrete spectra
Electrons are treated as quantum objects

externalPrerequisites.subject: Chemie
externalPrerequisites.concept: orbital model of the atom
externalPrerequisites.reason: Chemistry uses orbitals to explain bonding

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Postulates of Special Relativity
topics.description: Einstein's two postulates state that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames and that the speed of light is the same for all observers. Pupils explain how the Michelson–Morley result supports the constancy of c and why simultaneity becomes relative.
evidence: States the two postulates of special relativity
Explains why adding velocities "classically" fails for light
Explains with a thought experiment (train and lightning) why simultaneity depends on the observer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} imagines shining a torch forward from a very fast rocket, can they explain why the light is not faster than c?

prerequisites.reason: Relative velocities are the classical starting point
Light as electromagnetic radiation with speed c

topics.laenderNotes: Only a suggested extension in the KMK standards. NRW (Einführungsphase) and Bayern (Kl. 11 project work) treat it for all; Berlin-Brandenburg only in the Leistungskurs; BW as an elective topic; absent in Niedersachsen.

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Time Dilation and Length Contraction
topics.description: Using a light clock and Pythagoras, pupils derive that moving clocks run slow by the factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) and that moving lengths contract. They apply this to muons from cosmic rays and to the corrections needed for GPS satellites.
evidence: Derives the time dilation factor with a light clock
Explains why cosmic-ray muons reach the ground despite their short lifetime
Calculates time dilation for a satellite or particle and judges when it matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that GPS would be wrong by kilometres without relativity, can they explain which effect is responsible?

prerequisites.reason: Time dilation follows from the constancy of c

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: Pythagorean theorem
externalPrerequisites.reason: The light-clock derivation uses Pythagoras

topics.subject: Physik
topics.name: Relativistic Momentum and E = mc²
topics.description: At speeds close to c, momentum and energy grow without limit: p = γ·m·v and E = γ·m·c², so no massive particle reaches c. Pupils use the rest energy E₀ = m·c² and the relativistic energy of electrons in accelerators, and explain why a cyclotron fails for very fast particles.
evidence: Explains why the speed of light cannot be reached by accelerating a particle
Calculates the speed of an electron accelerated through 1 MV relativistically and classically and compares
Uses E₀ = m·c² to relate rest mass and energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an electron gains 1 MeV in an accelerator, can {{name}} show that the classical formula would give a speed faster than light, and correct it?

prerequisites.reason: Uses the factor γ
Generalises classical momentum
Electrons are accelerated by electric fields

topics.laenderNotes: Leistungskurs in NRW (cyclotron) and Berlin-Brandenburg; Bayern treats relativistic momentum at both levels in Kl. 12.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to turn measurements into graphs, spot proportional relationships and say how precise a measured value really is.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, Messwerte in Diagramme umzusetzen, proportionale Zusammenhänge zu erkennen und anzugeben, wie genau ein Messwert wirklich ist.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is learning that physics explains the world with models that have limits, and how to weigh physics facts and personal values when making decisions such as choosing a heating system.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, dass Physik die Welt mit Modellen erklärt, die Grenzen haben, und wie man bei Entscheidungen, etwa über eine Heizung, physikalische Fakten und eigene Werte abwägt.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager plans experiments from a hypothesis, evaluates them with linearised graphs and regression, and judges how uncertainties affect the result, as the Abitur requires.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind plant Experimente ausgehend von einer Hypothese, wertet sie mit linearisierten Diagrammen und Regression aus und beurteilt, wie Messunsicherheiten das Ergebnis beeinflussen, so wie es das Abitur verlangt.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how mirrors, lenses and prisms change the path of light, how the eye and spectacles work, and why screens mix colours from red, green and blue.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Spiegel, Linsen und Prismen den Weg des Lichts verändern, wie Auge und Brille funktionieren und warum Bildschirme Farben aus Rot, Grün und Blau mischen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is placing light, mobile-phone radiation and X-rays in one electromagnetic spectrum and using it to understand Earth's radiation budget and the greenhouse effect.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind ordnet Licht, Mobilfunkstrahlung und Röntgenstrahlung in ein gemeinsames elektromagnetisches Spektrum ein und versteht damit den Strahlungshaushalt der Erde und den Treibhauseffekt.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is exploring the solar system, explaining moon phases and eclipses with models, and learning how far away the stars are and how they live and die.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erkundet das Sonnensystem, erklärt Mondphasen und Finsternisse mit Modellen und erfährt, wie weit die Sterne entfernt sind und wie sie entstehen und vergehen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to describe motion with speed and graphs, to measure and draw forces, to tell mass from weight, and to explain levers, pressure and why ships float.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, Bewegungen mit Geschwindigkeit und Diagrammen zu beschreiben, Kräfte zu messen und zu zeichnen, Masse und Gewichtskraft zu unterscheiden und Hebel, Druck und das Schwimmen von Schiffen zu erklären.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is calculating with Newton's second law, friction and projectile motion, and using momentum to explain recoil, collisions and why airbags save lives.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind rechnet mit dem Newtonschen Grundgesetz, mit Reibung und dem waagerechten Wurf und erklärt mit dem Impuls Rückstoß, Stöße und warum Airbags Leben retten.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager analyses circular motion, Newton's law of gravitation and Kepler's laws, for example to calculate satellite orbits.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind analysiert Kreisbewegungen, das Gravitationsgesetz und die Keplerschen Gesetze und berechnet damit zum Beispiel Satellitenbahnen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is following energy through swings, roller coasters and machines, learning that it is conserved but partly "lost" as heat, and comparing devices by power and efficiency.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind verfolgt Energie bei Schaukel, Achterbahn und Maschinen, lernt, dass sie erhalten bleibt, aber teilweise als Wärme „verloren“ geht, und vergleicht Geräte nach Leistung und Wirkungsgrad.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is calculating energy balances and learning how power stations, wind and solar energy and storage technologies supply society with electricity.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind stellt Energiebilanzen auf und lernt, wie Kraftwerke, Wind- und Sonnenenergie und Speichertechniken die Gesellschaft mit Strom versorgen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is using the particle model to explain temperature and internal energy, calculating heating energy and learning how engines and heat pumps work.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erklärt Temperatur und innere Energie mit dem Teilchenmodell, berechnet Heizenergien und lernt, wie Motoren und Wärmepumpen funktionieren.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is measuring current and voltage, calculating with resistance and Ohm's law, working out electricity costs and learning how household wiring keeps people safe.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind misst Stromstärke und Spannung, rechnet mit Widerstand und Ohmschem Gesetz, ermittelt Stromkosten und lernt, wie die Hausinstallation Menschen schützt.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how electric motors, generators and transformers work through electromagnetism and induction, and how semiconductors power LEDs and solar cells.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Elektromotor, Generator und Transformator durch Elektromagnetismus und Induktion funktionieren und wie Halbleiter LEDs und Solarzellen ermöglichen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your child is learning what atomic nuclei are made of, how radioactive radiation is detected and shielded, what half-life means and how fission and fusion release energy.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, woraus Atomkerne bestehen, wie man radioaktive Strahlung nachweist und abschirmt, was Halbwertszeit bedeutet und wie Kernspaltung und Kernfusion Energie freisetzen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager describes radioactive decay with exponential functions, explains nuclear energy with mass defect and binding energy, and meets the Standard Model of particle physics.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind beschreibt den radioaktiven Zerfall mit Exponentialfunktionen, erklärt Kernenergie mit Massendefekt und Bindungsenergie und lernt das Standardmodell der Teilchenphysik kennen.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager works with the field concept: electric field strength, capacitors, magnetic flux density, the Lorentz force on moving charges and the law of induction, partly at Leistungskurs level.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind arbeitet mit dem Feldbegriff: elektrische Feldstärke, Kondensator, magnetische Flussdichte, Lorentzkraft auf bewegte Ladungen und Induktionsgesetz, teils auf Leistungskursniveau.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager describes pendulums and oscillating circuits as harmonic oscillations and uses interference at the double slit and grating to measure the wavelength of light.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind beschreibt Pendel und Schwingkreise als harmonische Schwingungen und misst mit Interferenz an Doppelspalt und Gitter die Wellenlänge von Licht.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager explores how light and electrons behave both as particles and as waves, what is random in quantum physics, and how energy levels explain the spectra of atoms.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht, wie sich Licht und Elektronen sowohl als Teilchen als auch als Wellen verhalten, was in der Quantenphysik zufällig ist und wie Energieniveaus die Spektren der Atome erklären.

clusters.subject: Physik
clusters.summary: Your teenager learns why the speed of light is the same for everyone, why moving clocks run slow, and why GPS needs Einstein's theory.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, warum die Lichtgeschwindigkeit für alle gleich ist, warum bewegte Uhren langsamer gehen und warum GPS ohne Einsteins Theorie nicht funktionieren würde.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how text, images and sound are stored as numbers, how spreadsheets calculate and analyse data, and how databases organise records.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Texte, Bilder und Töne als Zahlen gespeichert werden, wie Tabellenkalkulationen rechnen und Daten auswerten und wie Datenbanken Datensätze ordnen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is querying databases with SQL and learning how files are made smaller by compression.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind fragt Datenbanken mit SQL ab und lernt, wie Dateien durch Kompression kleiner werden.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager designs relational databases with ER diagrams, keys and normal forms and writes SQL queries across several tables.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind entwirft relationale Datenbanken mit ER-Diagrammen, Schlüsseln und Normalformen und schreibt SQL-Abfragen über mehrere Tabellen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is moving from block-based coding to a text-based language such as Python, writing programs with variables, conditions and loops.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind wechselt von der Blockprogrammierung zu einer textbasierten Sprache wie Python und schreibt Programme mit Variablen, Verzweigungen und Schleifen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is structuring programs with functions and lists, searching and sorting data, and testing code systematically.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind gliedert Programme mit Unterprogrammen und Listen, sucht und sortiert Daten und testet Programme systematisch.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager uses recursion and divide-and-conquer, compares algorithms by efficiency, and in Leistungskurs courses works with graphs and concurrency.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind nutzt Rekursion und das Prinzip Teile und Herrsche, vergleicht Algorithmen nach ihrer Effizienz und arbeitet im Leistungskurs mit Graphen und Nebenläufigkeit.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to see documents and graphics as objects with attributes and methods that belong to classes.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, Dokumente und Grafiken als Objekte mit Attributen und Methoden zu sehen, die zu Klassen gehören.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is programming their own classes and modelling programs with UML class diagrams.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind programmiert eigene Klassen und modelliert Programme mit UML-Klassendiagrammen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager designs larger programs with inheritance, polymorphism and encapsulation.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind entwirft größere Programme mit Vererbung, Polymorphie und Datenkapselung.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager uses stacks, queues, linked lists and trees as building blocks of efficient programs.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind nutzt Stapel, Schlangen, verkettete Listen und Bäume als Bausteine effizienter Programme.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is modelling machines as automata and learning how machine learning and generative AI work, where they fail and why training data matter.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind modelliert Maschinen als Automaten und lernt, wie maschinelles Lernen und generative KI funktionieren, wo sie Fehler machen und warum die Trainingsdaten so wichtig sind.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager studies concrete machine-learning methods and neural networks and evaluates how good and how fair an AI model is.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt konkrete Verfahren des maschinellen Lernens und neuronale Netze kennen und bewertet, wie gut und wie fair ein KI-Modell ist.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager describes languages with grammars and automata and, at Leistungskurs level, explores what computers can never compute and which problems are too hard in practice.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind beschreibt Sprachen mit Grammatiken und Automaten und untersucht, besonders im Leistungskurs, was Computer grundsätzlich nicht berechnen können und welche Probleme praktisch zu schwer sind.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how the internet connects clients and servers, and is building small devices with sensors and microcontrollers.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie das Internet Clients und Server verbindet, und baut kleine Geräte mit Sensoren und Mikrocontrollern.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how web protocols such as DNS and HTTP work and how logic gates let computers calculate.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Internetprotokolle wie DNS und HTTP funktionieren und wie Computer mit logischen Schaltungen rechnen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager studies how a processor executes programs and how layered network protocols such as TCP/IP deliver data reliably.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht, wie ein Prozessor Programme ausführt und wie Netzwerkprotokolle im Schichtenmodell wie TCP/IP Daten zuverlässig übertragen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how simple ciphers are broken, how to secure accounts and backups, and how tracking works and what rights the DSGVO gives them.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie einfache Verschlüsselungen geknackt werden, wie man Konten und Daten sichert und wie Tracking funktioniert und welche Rechte die DSGVO gibt.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager learns how public-key cryptography, signatures and certificates secure the internet and applies data-protection principles to real cases.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie asymmetrische Verschlüsselung, Signaturen und Zertifikate das Internet absichern, und wendet die Grundsätze des Datenschutzes auf echte Fälle an.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is examining software licences, the power of large platforms and filter bubbles, and the environmental footprint of digital technology.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind setzt sich mit Softwarelizenzen, der Macht großer Plattformen und Informationsblasen sowie dem ökologischen Fußabdruck digitaler Technik auseinander.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager discusses how automation and AI change work and society and who is responsible when algorithms make decisions about people.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind diskutiert, wie Automatisierung und KI Arbeit und Gesellschaft verändern und wer verantwortlich ist, wenn Algorithmen über Menschen entscheiden.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is building web pages with HTML and CSS and learning to separate content from design.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erstellt Webseiten mit HTML und CSS und lernt, Inhalt und Gestaltung zu trennen.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how search engines find and rank pages, and why ranking is not the same as reliability.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Suchmaschinen Seiten finden und sortieren und warum ein guter Platz in der Trefferliste noch nichts über die Verlässlichkeit sagt.

clusters.subject: Informatik & Medienbildung
clusters.summary: Your teenager develops software in a team, sharing tasks, agreeing interfaces and using version control.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind entwickelt Software im Team, teilt Aufgaben auf, vereinbart Schnittstellen und nutzt eine Versionsverwaltung.
